articles.title: FastAPI vs Node.js vs Bun: One PostgreSQL Setting Was Worth Up to 31% (No Runtime Changed)
articles.description: Express beat Bun in one test. Bun nearly doubled Node in another. And one PostgreSQL setting was...
articles.body_html:
Express beat Bun in one test. Bun nearly doubled Node in another. And one PostgreSQL setting was worth up to 31% — with no runtime change at all. The interesting part isn't who won. It's why the winner keeps changing.

Imagine you're choosing the backend for a new application. You have three obvious options:

  • FastAPI — Python, async support, type validation, excellent developer experience.
  • Node.js — a mature JavaScript ecosystem with battle-tested database libraries.
  • Bun — a newer JavaScript runtime promising lower overhead and more speed.

You search for benchmarks. One says Bun is dramatically faster. Another says Node.js wins. A third makes FastAPI look painfully slow. Same general task, different winners.

So what are we actually measuring?

I went through several publicly available 2026 benchmarks — their configurations, their raw result tables, and their methodology. One finding reframed the whole question for me:

Changing how Node.js talks to PostgreSQL was worth up to 31% in a published benchmark — without changing the JavaScript runtime, the framework, or the database engine.

That's a big enough swing to flip a comparison. And it points at a better question than "Which backend is fastest?":

Are we comparing programming languages, HTTP frameworks, database drivers, or somebody's connection-pool configuration?

Let's follow the evidence.

Transparency: I did not run these performance tests myself. This article analyzes independently published 2026 benchmarks, and every measurement below is attributed to its source. Two tables marked hypothetical are explanatory examples, not data.

The short version, if you only read one section

Before the detail, here's how I'd actually decide — because "fastest in a chart" is rarely the deciding factor:

Your situation What I'd prioritize
Existing Python team, ML / data workloads FastAPI's ecosystem and integration
Existing TypeScript backend, mature infra Node.js and its library compatibility
New JS/TS service where resource efficiency matters Evaluate Bun against your actual workload
PostgreSQL-heavy CRUD Query design, indexes, pooling, and p99 — not the runtime
Strict response-time SLAs Repeatable, production-like load testing

Now, why the benchmarks disagree.

1. The numbers that started the argument

In October 2026, the framework-rps benchmark compared seven backend stacks. The task was deliberately tiny: accept an HTTP request, run SELECT 1 against PostgreSQL, return {"status":"ok"}.

Setting Configuration
Host Apple M1 Pro, 10 CPU cores, 16 GB
App container 2 CPUs, 2 GB
PostgreSQL 17 container 1 CPU, 1 GB, max_connections=200
Shared DB connection cap 50
Load generator k6, constant virtual users, 30s warm-up, 3× 30s measured
Date October 15, 2026

Each app ran one at a time, so the stacks never competed for CPU. Reported highest stable throughput (requests/sec):

Backend Requests/sec At p95
Express 5 / Node.js 24 21,604 25 VUs 2.1 ms
Bun 1.4 18,038 400 VUs 52.4 ms
Fastify 5 / Node.js 24 13,632 100 VUs 30.2 ms
FastAPI 0.143 / Python 3.14 8,821 25 VUs 5.0 ms

(The full benchmark also includes Go — which won outright at 24,690 — plus Spring Boot and Laravel. I'm focusing on the three stacks in the title.)

Highest stable throughput — requests/sec (higher is better)

Express  ████████████████████  21,604
Bun      █████████████████     18,038
Fastify  █████████████         13,632
FastAPI  ████████               8,821
Source: framework-rps, Oct 2026

Wait. Wasn't Bun supposed to beat Node?

Two things before anyone declares Express the champion.

First, these "best" numbers come from different concurrency levels. Express peaked at 25 virtual users (p95 2.1 ms); Bun peaked at 400 (p95 52.4 ms). That's not a comparison at the same offered load. At 25 VUs, the same benchmark records Bun at 16,432 RPS — a published row, not my estimate. So the honest reading is narrow:

On this machine, with these implementations and this SELECT 1 workload, Express sustained higher stable throughput than Bun. It does not prove Node is universally faster.

Second, look at Express versus Fastify. Express (21,604) beats Fastify (13,632) by ~58% — and both use the same driver (pg, simple-query protocol) on the same 2-CPU budget. Fastify is normally the faster of the two. Identical driver, identical budget, 58% apart, with Fastify never clearing ~13.6k at any concurrency level: that's not something framework overhead alone explains, and it's exactly the kind of result that should make you open the methodology before you quote the chart. I won't claim the benchmark is "wrong" — but that row deserves investigation, not a headline.

Source: framework-rps — full methodology and per-level results

2. In a different benchmark, Bun nearly doubled Node

A separate 2026 project, js-runtimes-benchmark, tested 22 JavaScript runtime × framework stacks against a full RealWorld app on an 8-vCPU box with a dedicated 16-vCPU PostgreSQL machine.

Its headline metric is sustained users — the most simulated users each stack held for five minutes under p95 < 500 ms, p99 < 1 s, < 1% errors — with requests/sec reported as a separate column. Those are not the same number, and conflating them is the exact trap this article is about, so here's the top of the table with both:

Implementation Sustained users Requests/sec
Bun · Bun.serve 84,000 21,469
Node · Fastify 46,000 12,181
Node · Express 40,000 10,530

By requests/sec, Bun delivered ~76% more throughput than Fastify here (the users column shows +83% — pick one unit and stick to it).

So which benchmark is right? Both — they're measuring different stacks on different hardware. And notice what doesn't survive the unit fix: benchmark 2's Bun did 21,469 RPS on an 8-vCPU box with a 16-vCPU database; benchmark 1's Express did 21,604 RPS on a 2-CPU container. By requests/sec they're nearly identical — on roughly four times the hardware. You cannot line up the absolute numbers from these two experiments at all. "Bun nearly doubled Node" is true inside benchmark 2 (same rig, Bun vs Node); it is meaningless across the two.

That is the whole problem with most runtime comparisons in one example: we take a measurement of an entire stack-plus-hardware and attribute it to a single component.

Let's isolate one of those components.

3. The PostgreSQL setting worth up to 31%

This was the most useful finding in the research. In the 22-stack benchmark, the author first used node-postgres (pg) the way most code does:

const result = await pool.query(
  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1",
  [userId]
);

Perfectly normal. But in this form pg sends an unnamed statement, which PostgreSQL re-parses and re-plans on every call. The author then switched to named prepared statements:

const result = await pool.query({
  name: "find-user-by-id",
  text: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1",
  values: [userId],
});

The name lets PostgreSQL reuse the prepared statement on that connection. Same runtime, same framework, same database — only the driver's statement handling changed.

Important: these figures are the benchmark's sustainable-user capacity (its headline metric), not raw RPS. Capacity and RPS move together here, but the number is users:

Node stack Default pg Named prepared Change
Express 39,000 40,000 +3%
Hono 35,000 39,000 +11%
Fastify 42,000 46,000 +10%
node:http 36,000 42,000 +17%
Ultimate Express 35,000 46,000 +31%

Source: js-runtimes-benchmark, section 3. Median across all Node stacks was +14%, with 30–37% less database CPU per request.

Two things to keep honest about this:

  • The gain was framework-specific. Ultimate Express jumped 31%; plain Express moved 3%, because Express was already its own bottleneck. "Node got 31% faster" would be the wrong lesson.
  • It didn't close the gap to Bun. The Node stacks stayed CPU-limited on the app box; prepared statements cut database CPU, not Node's. Bun (via Bun.SQL) and the Deno stacks (via postgres.js) prepare automatically, so the default-pg Node rows were carrying a tax the others never paid.

Which is the real point:

A runtime benchmark can contain a large database-client effect even when the HTTP application looks identical. Comparing Node + pg (unnamed) against Bun + Bun.SQL (auto-prepared) isn't just V8 vs JavaScriptCore — it's two database-access implementations with different defaults.

4. The database can hide the runtime — or expose it

Here's where I'd push back on a common oversimplification ("add a database and all runtimes converge"). Whether that's true depends entirely on how much work the database does.

Regime A — trivial query (SELECT 1). The database computes almost nothing. HTTP routing, the PostgreSQL wire protocol, driver behavior, and scheduling make up a large share of each request. Runtime and driver differences are highly visible — which is exactly why section 1's stacks spread so far apart. That benchmark is closer to a runtime-and-driver test than a "database" test.

Regime B — expensive query (joins, sorts, large result sets). Now consider an illustrative request (hypothetical numbers, to show the shape — not measured data):

Operation Example duration
HTTP routing + validation 0.3 ms
Waiting for a connection 0.5 ms
Database / network work 8.0 ms
Decode rows + serialize JSON 0.7 ms
Total 9.5 ms

Halve the routing cost and you save 0.15 ms — a 1.6% improvement to the whole request. That's Amdahl's law: speeding up a small slice barely moves the total.

So both can be true. A trivial query exposes the runtime; an expensive one can bury it. The database doesn't erase runtime differences — it changes where they show up. (A separate 2026 Bun vs Node comparison on DEV found Bun kept a real edge on a local PostgreSQL route, consistent with Regime A.)

5. FastAPI needs a fairer comparison too

So far Python looks like the loser. But there's a gap between measuring FastAPI's framework overhead and measuring a production-style FastAPI app.

FastAPI runs ordinary def endpoints in a thread pool and async def endpoints as coroutines on the event loop (official docs). An async endpoint over an async driver like asyncpg behaves very differently from a sync endpoint over a sync driver — and worker count matters just as much. Comparing one FastAPI process against a multi-process Node setup answers a different question than comparing production configurations of both. Both are legitimate; they just aren't the same experiment.

And the ORM can cost more than the language. The small-runtime-bench project, run on dedicated 16-vCPU cloud machines, measured each stack through its real ORM versus the raw driver:

  • SQLAlchemy cut FastAPI throughput ~57%
  • Prisma cut NestJS ~48%
  • Django's ORM cost ~30%
  • ActiveRecord was nearly free (0–2%)

That doesn't make SQLAlchemy "bad" — ORMs buy you models, relationships, portability, and ergonomics. But it means you cannot compare FastAPI-with-an-ORM against Node-with-raw-SQL against Bun-with-a-native-client and announce you've isolated the fastest language. You've measured three application stacks. That's useful — as long as you call it what it is.

Source: small-runtime-bench — ORM-tax methodology and results

6. The hidden variable: connection pooling

Say your app gets 500 concurrent requests and your pool allows 20 connections. The other 480 wait — and waiting time hits your users exactly like query time does. Now compare three apps configured like this:

Stack Pool size
FastAPI 10
Node.js 20
Bun 50

One wins. Can you attribute that to the runtime? No — the larger pool might help one workload and overload PostgreSQL on another. A controlled comparison tests identical connection limits first, then sweeps pool size (5 → 10 → 20 → 50), measuring completed RPS, p95/p99, connection wait, database CPU, and errors at each step.

One more trap: the limit is per pool instance. Four workers with a pool of 20 each is up to 80 database connections, and PostgreSQL has its own connection and memory ceiling. A config that's harmless for one process gets expensive when scaled — which is why the fastest app config and the fastest database config have to be chosen together.

7. RPS can hide a collapsing service

The question I'd ask of any benchmark chart: what happened to the requests that didn't finish?

Metric Service A Service B
Completed RPS 20,000 18,000
p95 latency 900 ms 35 ms
p99 latency 2,500 ms 70 ms
Error rate 2.0% 0%

(Hypothetical, to illustrate.) Service A "wins" on throughput. Would you ship it for a latency-sensitive API? A system under overload can post an impressive RPS headline while quietly queueing and erroring.

This is also where the load model matters — and where I'll be honest about the benchmarks above. There are two models:

  • Closed-loop: each virtual user waits for a response before sending the next. If the server slows down, the offered rate automatically falls, which can hide overload behavior.
  • Open-loop: new work arrives on a fixed schedule regardless of whether prior work finished — which exposes what happens when traffic keeps coming and responses slow.

Grafana k6 supports both; its constant-arrival-rate executor is the open-loop one:

import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    database_read: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 1000, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "60s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 200, maxVUs: 1000,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<200"],
    dropped_iterations: ["count==0"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/users/42`);
  check(res, { "status is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Worth flagging: both benchmarks I've leaned on here are closed-loop (constant virtual users / think-time visitors). They're carefully run — both warm up, and the second does two-minute capacity probes and five-minute sustained holds — but the closed-loop model is the one with the blind spot I just described. If you reproduce any of this, add an open-loop run and watch dropped_iterations (k6 reports these when it can't launch scheduled work). A benchmark should distinguish offered, sent, and completed traffic — that distinction often matters more than the biggest number in the chart.

Sources: k6 open vs closed models, dropped iterations.

8. What a fair FastAPI vs Node vs Bun test would look like

I wouldn't start with a single winner-takes-all number. I'd split it into two questions.

Experiment A — which application stack handles the workload best? Realistic, idiomatic implementations:

Stack HTTP server DB client
FastAPI Uvicorn asyncpg
Node.js Fastify node-postgres
Bun Bun.serve Bun.SQL

Same schema, query semantics, indexes, response shape, and resource budget — and document the statement handling, because section 3 shows it moves the number.

Experiment B — how much is the runtime vs the client? Add controls that hold the runtime constant and vary the driver (Fastify on Node and Bun with the same postgres.js; pg unnamed vs named). Then run five increasingly realistic workloads:

Test What it reveals
JSON only HTTP + serialization overhead
SELECT 1 Minimal DB round trip (Regime A)
Indexed lookup Basic real-data read
100-row query Decode + serialization cost
Mixed read/write Transactions, contention, pool behavior (Regime B)

The rule is: don't change five variables at once. If Bun wins JSON but loses mixed read/write, that's a bottleneck to investigate, not proof one runtime is "better."

My minimum checklist before trusting results for a production decision: fixed versions/hardware/DB settings/dataset; comparable worker counts and connection budgets; correctness tests per endpoint before timing; warm-up plus repeated runs with variability reported; identical offered load and a capacity search; p50/p95/p99, throughput, errors, and dropped work; CPU/memory/DB-utilization/pool metrics; and a repo with source, config, and raw results. Excessive for a blog post — not excessive for an architecture decision.

9. So which would I choose?

Not from these benchmarks alone. The table at the top is how I'd actually weigh it — but the deciding factors usually aren't in any RPS chart. If one stack serves the same traffic with fewer instances or more latency headroom, that's real operational money. But application economics also include migrations, debugging, libraries, deployment, and the familiarity of the team that has to run it at 3 a.m. A stack that's 30% faster in a synthetic test isn't automatically 30% cheaper to operate — and it certainly won't make your developers 30% more productive.

10. The result that changed how I read benchmarks

The finding that stuck with me wasn't Express hitting 21,604 RPS, or Bun sustaining 84,000 users in a different test, or FastAPI trailing. It was this:

One published experiment changed a stack's capacity by up to 31% just by naming its prepared statements.

The runtime didn't change. The framework didn't change. The database engine didn't change. A detail in the database-access layer did — and it was enough to reorder stacks.

A benchmark tells you what was fastest under its conditions. Understanding the conditions tells you whether the result applies to your application.

That's the part I'd read before rewriting a backend — and the part I wish more framework comparisons put in their headline instead of a chart with three bars.

Sources

  1. framework-rps — Oct 2026 PostgreSQL API benchmark; container limits, per-concurrency throughput and latency.
  2. js-runtimes-benchmark — 22 JS stacks; sustained-users metric, prepared-statement experiment, CPU observations. (The authors note one grid had ~5% background-CPU contamination affecting the Bun rows, and run-to-run spread of ~±5% — read close results as ranges.)
  3. small-runtime-bench — multi-runtime ORM-tax measurement and reproducibility methodology.
  4. Bun SQL docs · 5. node-postgres docs · 6. FastAPI async docs · 7. k6 constant-arrival-rate · 8. Bun vs Node 2026 (DEV).

Tables reproduce or compute from these published measurements; the two tables marked hypothetical are explanatory.

One question for the comments: have you ever changed a database driver, pool size, or ORM config and seen a bigger improvement than switching frameworks? I'm especially interested in cases where the benchmark winner changed once a real database entered the picture.

articles.title: 61 Hackathons, 2,000+ GitHub Contributions: The Free Chrome Planner That Keeps Me Shipping
articles.description: We have all been there.  You sign up for one hackathon. Then a friend sends another one with a cool...
articles.body_html:
We have all been there.

You sign up for one hackathon. Then a friend sends another one with a cool theme. Meanwhile, you still have a side project and a regular work sprint. On paper, everything looks doable — until two deadlines land in the same week, your weekends disappear, and you realize you haven't had a single real day off all month.

Regular calendars are great at showing when things happen, but they never stop you from overbooking yourself. They don't care if two sprints collide or if your rest buffer drops to zero.

So I built Dev Cadence — a free, open-source Chrome Side Panel extension I use every day to plan my own sprints, hackathons, and rest days.

No accounts. No subscriptions. No tracking.

Why I built this

If you check my profile, you'll see I've participated in around 61 hackathons across Devpost, DEV.to, DevSpot, NASA and other platforms. For a long time, I tried tracking everything in Excel and regular calendars — Excel gave me dates without a visual picture, and calendars never gave me a quick color-coded view of my actual sprint load.

I wanted a small control center for work that has a real start date, end date, and deadline, where I could open it for 2 seconds and immediately know: what's busy, what's free, and can I realistically take on another sprint?

On October 1, 2026, I built the first version of Dev Cadence for myself as a Chrome Side Panel extension. Here's the live stream review of the first version where the hosts broke down the design. I used it every day through October and November, writing down every rough edge I ran into.

In October, putting all my hackathons into those color-coded cells gave me a reality check: I had zero rest days and no space for other work — no way to ship a quality MVP like that. Looking at my statuses, I saw which events were still just Interest or Join with no early submission yet, dropped a few without pain, and finished every single project I committed to (on my Devpost profile, my registered and submitted counts match).

The built-in analytics showed me how heavy October had been, so I adjusted my pace and expanded the extension beyond hackathons to cover personal sprints, side projects, and regular dev work.

When I joined a Hybrid AI hackathon in November, I added two optional AI features while keeping the extension privacy-first: your schedule stays in your browser (with manual JSON export/import), and you never have to touch AI if you prefer filling dates manually. If you do want automatic deadline extraction and sprint pace advice, you can download Chrome's ~4 GB on-device Gemini Nano model in one click so prompts stay local on your device — or let the extension fall back to cloud Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

Why Projects Stall (and How Dev Cadence Evolved)

I hold a Master's degree in Management and Administration, so I pay close attention to why good projects stall. Across hackathons and side projects, I kept seeing the same gap: tons of people register with great ideas, yet very few actually cross the finish line. Usually it's not a lack of coding skill — it's not seeing the big picture of your own schedule while you're deciding what to take on.

With 2,000+ GitHub contributions over the past year while building under tough everyday conditions, I'm my own strictest test user. If you're curious to see how the extension evolved from a simple local tracker into a Hybrid AI planner:

  • Version 1 (Before): Dev Cadence on Devpost.
  • Version 2 (Now): Dev Cadence AI on Devpost — rebuilt for universal sprint planning with optional Hybrid AI.

What Dev Cadence does

Because it lives in the Chrome Side Panel, you can open it right next to any hackathon page, GitHub repo, or issue tracker without switching tabs.

  • Spot date overlaps immediately: When two sprints land on the same days, calendar cells split diagonally in both colors so you see the collision at a glance.
  • Protect your rest days: A bottom capacity bar tracks your month in real time — Build, Free, and Rest days against your personal monthly rest goal.
  • Stop copy-pasting deadlines: Open any event or project page, click Extract from Page, and Dev Cadence reads the active tab on demand to fill in the title, URL, and deadline for you.
  • Get a friendly nudge when you overbook: When sprints overlap or your rest days dip below target, the AI Pace Advisor gives a short, human reminder on what to prioritize first — and when to take a breather.
  • Transparent & under your control: Every AI response clearly shows an On-Device or Cloud badge, and you can stop generation or switch back to manual entry anytime.
  • Clean daily workspace: Card and Table tracker views, monthly pace analytics, 3 themes (Warm Vellum, Obsidian Brass, Ocean Slate), and font size scaling.

Try it for free

👉 Install Dev Cadence from the Chrome Web Store

It takes 5 seconds to install, works out of the box with zero sign-up, and stays out of your way until you need it.

Curious about how the Hybrid AI architecture works under the hood (or want to inspect/fork the code)? Everything is open source under Apache 2.0 — check out the technical breakdown in the GitHub README.

How do you keep yourself from overbooking side projects and hackathons? Drop your workflow (or feedback on the extension) in the comments — I'd love to hear what works for you.

articles.title: My password generator used crypto.getRandomValues and was still wrong 15% of the time
articles.description: My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z,...
articles.body_html:
My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, symbols) and crypto.getRandomValues. I assumed it was done. Then I went back to it while writing a blog post, and it had two problems. One was mostly theoretical. The other was very practical.

The original code 

let s = '';
if (up.checked) s += 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
if (lo.checked) s += 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz';
if (nu.checked) s += '0123456789';
if (sy.checked) s += '!@#$%^&*()-_=+[]{};:,.?';

const a = new Uint32Array(L);
crypto.getRandomValues(a);
let p = '';
for (let i = 0; i < L; i++) p += s[a[i] % s.length];

It uses a cryptographic RNG, so it looks fine. Here's what's wrong with it.

Problem 1: "Password must contain a number"

Ticking "0–9" only means digits are allowed. Nothing guarantees one shows up. With all four groups ticked, the combined set has 85 characters, and only 10 of them are digits.

I simulated 200,000 passwords at each length and counted how many were missing at least one of the ticked groups:

Length Missing a ticked group
6 70.6%
8 51.0%
12 26.5%
16 (my default) 14.6%

So roughly one in seven passwords at the default length would be rejected by a sign-up form that requires "at least one number and one symbol". The user ticked the boxes, copied the password, and the website said no. That's a real bug, not a theory.

Problem 2: modulo bias

a[i] % s.length maps 2³² possible values onto 85 characters. 2³² isn't a multiple of 85 (the remainder is 1), so one character gets picked very slightly more often than the others. Here the difference is about 2 in 10 billion, which nobody will ever exploit. But the fix is three lines, and it matters more when the set size is large relative to the random range. So:

// unbiased integer in [0, n)
function rnd(n) {
  const lim = Math.floor(2 ** 32 / n) * n;   // largest multiple of n
  const b = new Uint32Array(1);
  do { crypto.getRandomValues(b); } while (b[0] >= lim);
  return b[0] % n;
}

This is rejection sampling: throw away the few values from the incomplete top range and draw again. For small n a retry almost never happens.

The fix for problem 1

Pick one character from each ticked group first, fill the rest from the combined set, then shuffle so the guaranteed characters aren't always at the start:

const sets = [];   // only the ticked groups
// ...push each ticked group's characters...
const all = sets.join('');

const c = sets.map(g => g[rnd(g.length)]);   // one from each group
while (c.length < L) c.push(all[rnd(all.length)]);

for (let i = c.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {     // Fisher–Yates
  const j = rnd(i + 1);
  [c[i], c[j]] = [c[j], c[i]];
}
const password = c.join('');

I ran 20,000 passwords of length 6 with all groups ticked through the new version. All 20,000 contained every group.

Does guaranteeing one of each make the passwords weaker? Slightly, in theory, because the space is a little smaller than "any 16 of 85". In practice it's negligible. A 16-character password with all four groups is still around 100 bits of entropy, and the alternative is a password the website refuses.

The lesson

Using crypto.getRandomValues makes a generator secure. It doesn't make it correct. The bug that hurt users was in the logic around the RNG: what the checkboxes promise versus what the code guarantees. If you've written a generator like this, run a quick simulation over its output. It takes five minutes.

The generator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. Nothing you generate is sent anywhere.

articles.title: Resurrecting HyperCard for the browser with Kiro — PhantomCard
articles.description: For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's...
articles.body_html:
For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's HyperCard that runs entirely in your browser. Stack of cards, buttons, fields, a working HyperTalk interpreter, System-7 monochrome chrome — no build step, no dependencies, just ES modules.

Try it live: https://till3005.github.io/phantomcard/ · Code: https://github.com/Till3005/phantomcard

Why HyperCard, and why "resurrection"?

Kiroween's Resurrection category asks you to bring dead technology back to life. HyperCard (1987) was the first mass-market hypermedia tool: a stack of "cards" holding buttons, fields and paint, scripted in HyperTalk — English-ish code like answer "Hello" with "OK" and go to next card. Entire generations learned programming by clicking around someone else's stack. Apple killed it in 2004, and browsers never quite replaced the magic of "open a stack, flip through cards, tweak a button's script."

PhantomCard resurrects that loop: you can flip through bundled demo stacks (a welcome tour, a séance deck, a haunted-house adventure), then hit Authoring mode and add a button, type its HyperTalk script, and watch it actually run.

How Kiro shaped the build

This is where Kiro stopped being a code generator and started being a collaborator:

  • Spec-driven development. Before a line of app code existed, we wrote the spec in .kiro/specs/phantomcard/: requirements (data model, HyperTalk grammar surface, interaction modes), a design doc, and a task list. When the agent drifted — proposing a React scaffold or a build step — the spec pulled it back. Every judgment call I made later traced to a spec decision, not a chat message.
  • Steering rules. .kiro/steering/ holds the rules Kiro worked under: zero build step, ES modules only, System-7 visual fidelity, no dependencies beyond lz-string. Those constraints are the reason the app loads instantly on GitHub Pages and the codebase stays readable end-to-end.
  • The HyperTalk interpreter — the hardest part — was co-written with Kiro CLI: a lexer, a recursive-descent parser, and an async interpreter with re-entrant send/dispatch semantics. Kiro wrote the grammar tests that caught edge cases (e.g. item idx of omens after put c + 1 into c).

What's in the box

  • 512×342 canvas-rendered cards with dissolve transitions (faithful to the original)
  • Buttons, fields, paint layers, custom Chrome menus and dialogs — all monochrome System 7
  • A real HyperTalk runtime: handlers, put/get/go/answer/ask, item/line chunks, the number of cards
  • URL-shareable stacks (state compressed into the link via lz-string)
  • Three demo stacks authored as HyperCard docs: Welcome, The Séance Deck, The Haunted House

What I'd do differently

The trickiest bug: a "dissolve" animation re-fired on every render, not just card changes — the fix was a one-line guard on the card id, found by watching a screen recording of the app in frame-by-frame. Retro-faithful doesn't mean stateless.

PhantomCard is MIT-licensed and in the running for Kiroween 2026's Resurrection category. If you grew up on HyperCard — or never got to — go flip a stack.

articles.title: The "LGTM" Epidemic: Why Your Code Reviews Are Just Rubber Stamps
articles.description: Imagine this. It’s Tuesday morning. You’re sipping your coffee, feeling good. Then, the Slack...
articles.body_html:
Imagine this. It’s Tuesday morning. You’re sipping your coffee, feeling good. Then, the Slack notification hits: a P1 incident. Production is down.

You jump into the war room. Everyone is panicking. You dig through the logs, trace the stack trace, and finally find the culprit. It’s a stupidly simple bug. A missing null check. Or a wrong variable name.

Then comes the gut punch: you check the Git history. This code was merged two weeks ago. It had been approved by three senior engineers. The PR had a green checkmark. The tests passed.

How did this happen?

Because everyone just commented "LGTM" and moved on with their day.

We’ve all been there. I’ve been there. I’ve been the one who approved a 500-line PR in 45 seconds because I was rushing to my next meeting. But this "Looks Good To Me" culture is slowly rotting our codebases, and we need to talk about it.

The illusion of "Four Eyes"

The whole point of code review is to catch what the author missed. It’s supposed to be a safety net. But in reality, it often becomes a performative ritual.

Why do we do it?

  1. The Bottleneck Fear: Nobody wants to be the guy who blocks a release because of a minor naming convention. We feel pressured to approve quickly so the team can ship.
  2. Cognitive Overload: If you send me a PR with 40 changed files, my brain just shuts down. I can’t review that properly, so I just scan it and hit approve, hoping for the best.
  3. The "It Compiles" Mentality: If the CI/CD pipeline is green and the tests pass, we assume it works. We forget that tests only prove the code does what the author thought it should do — not what it actually needs to do.

The math of the "Rubber Stamp"

Let's look at the uncomfortable reality of how we actually review code versus how we think we do:

PR Size (Lines of Code) Average Review Time Actual Review Quality
1 - 50 lines 15 - 30 mins High. Real questions are asked.
50 - 200 lines 10 - 15 mins Medium. Major logic is checked, edge cases ignored.
200 - 500 lines 5 - 8 mins Low. Skimming for typos.
500+ lines < 2 mins LGTM. (Please just let me close this tab).

When a PR gets too big, the reviewer’s brain switches from "analytical" to "survival mode". We stop looking for logic errors and start looking for reasons to just approve it and move on.

A code review is not a proofreading session

Here is what a typical "LGTM" review looks like in the wild:

+ // Adding a new caching layer for user profiles
+ const user = await getUserFromCache(userId);
+ if (user) {
+    return user; 
+ }
+ // Fallback to DB
+ const dbUser = await fetchFromDB(userId);
+ await setUserInCache(userId, dbUser);
+ return dbUser;

The Reviewer: "LGTM 👍" (Approved).

What the reviewer missed: dbUser could be null if the user doesn't exist, which means we are caching null and returning it, causing a silent failure on the frontend three calls later.

The author had all the context in their head, so it looked fine to them. The reviewer just glanced at the syntax, saw that it "makes sense", and approved it.

How do we fix the "LGTM" epidemic?
I don't think the answer is "just be more careful." That's like telling someone to "just be happier." We need structural changes.

1. Ban the LGTM comment.
Seriously. Make it a team rule. If you are approving a PR, you must leave a comment explaining what you checked. Even if it’s just: "Checked the DB calls and the error handling looks correct. Tested locally, works as expected." This forces the reviewer's brain to actually engage with the code, even for a few seconds.

2. Enforce the 200-line rule.
If a PR is over 200 lines of actual logic (excluding generated files, lockfiles, etc.), it gets rejected automatically. It must be split. Reviewing smaller chunks is the only way to maintain quality without burning out your seniors.

3. Ask a real question.
The best code reviews are the ones where the reviewer asks, "Why did you choose this approach instead of X?" or "What happens if this API call times out?" If you can't think of a single question to ask about a PR, it probably means you didn't read it carefully enough.

4. The "Rubber Duck" review.
Before you assign a reviewer, explain your own PR in the comments. Write a short paragraph: "Hey, this PR does X. The tricky part was Y, so I handled it by doing Z. Please pay special attention to the database transaction on line 45." This guides the reviewer exactly where to look and prevents them from getting lost.

It’s about culture, not tools
You can have the fanciest CI/CD pipeline, the most strict linters, and the best AI code review bots (yes, even Claude or Copilot). But if your human reviewers are just acting as a human LGTM button, your codebase is a ticking time bomb.

Code reviews are not a gate to pass; they are a conversation about the code. And a conversation requires more than just saying "Looks good."

Let's discuss
I'm curious how other teams handle this.

Do you have a team culture where it’s acceptable to block a PR for a whole day just to ask questions?

What is your "hard limit" for PR size before you hit that reject button?

Have you ever caught a catastrophic bug in a review that the CI completely missed? What was it?

I'd love to hear your war stories. Because at the end of the day, the best code review is the one that prevents you from getting that 3 AM PagerDuty alert.

articles.title: “Can you send me the staging password again?” Why I built Global Login
articles.description: We kept sharing passwords internally. Someone needed to test a project, so one of us sent them the...
articles.body_html:
We kept sharing passwords internally. Someone needed to test a project, so one of us sent them the login. A few days later, someone else needed it. By then we had a second question to answer: was that the staging password or the production one?

What bothered me was how ordinary the interruption felt. A teammate could have the site open, know exactly what they wanted to test, and still have to wait for another person to reply.

That’s the problem I built Global Login to solve. It gives our team a shared place for project accounts and brings the right choices into the browser when someone needs to sign in.

Start with the project

Say you’re checking a fix before it goes live. You know the project name and you know you want staging. Those two details should be enough. On the dashboard, each project keeps its accounts together, so you can give the test account a label that the next person will recognize.

Meet people at the sign-in field

Here’s my favorite part. Open the project site in Chrome and click the sign-in field. The extension shows matching accounts. Pick the one you need and it fills the form. If you’re starting in the extension, Open & Fill takes you to the saved site.

That changes the handoff. I can tell a teammate “use the staging account in Global Login,” and that answer still makes sense after the password changes. When the extension suggests saving an update, someone gets to review it first.

Leave room for the things that belong to one person

Building a shared vault raised a very human question for me: if I put something here, who can see it? Project accounts belong in the team workspace. My private vault is for things like my own API credentials and secure notes. Even a file I attach to a shared login stays private to me. That’s a small distinction I’d want to understand before uploading anything.

What you can do with Global Login

When you need to… Here’s what you can do
Find the right environment Keep local, staging, and production accounts under one project. Tag and sort logins, group projects into collections, and refresh their website icons individually or in bulk.
Sign in to a project site Pick a matching account in the sign-in field, search other logins with the keyboard, or use Open & Fill. Review suggested saves and updates. Exclude a site or switch off the floating prompt when you want to.
Test a new signup Generate a fresh password, fill identity fields from a saved profile, or open the external temporary-mailbox shortcut.
Keep personal details handy Use your private vault’s 21 item types for things like API credentials, identities, cards, SSH keys, and secure notes.
Attach a file Upload, rename, download, or delete files up to 50 MiB each. A document can reference a file. Attaching one to a shared login still leaves access with its owner.
Bring a teammate onboard An administrator approves membership and controls edit and backup permissions. A view-only teammate can still use shared logins for testing.
Find out what changed A login’s activity history shows who updated it and when, including changes made through an AI client.
Automate housekeeping Connect an AI client through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) using a personal token. It can organize collections, refresh icons, or manage vault items and files within your permissions.
Back up or self-host Authorized members can export shared projects and accounts. Imports require backup and edit permissions. You can also run the workspace on your own Cloudflare account.

What happens to a password when I click Save?

The server encrypts each project password with AES-256-GCM before writing it to the database. It uses a fresh random value each time and binds the encrypted password to its account ID. Someone who gets a copy of the database would also need the server’s encryption key to read those passwords. Moving an encrypted password to a different account record would fail the integrity check. Read the encryption code.

Access matters just as much as encryption. A workspace administrator approves new members. Approved teammates can use shared accounts, while the server checks ownership for personal vault items. The server can decrypt passwords to deliver them for autofill, so the people running the workspace and protecting its encryption key are part of the trust model. See the private vault implementation.

One detail matters when you make a backup. An authorized export contains readable shared passwords, so whoever holds the exported file can read them. The encryption shown above protects the database copy.

The tech stack behind it

I used TypeScript across the project and React for both the web dashboard and the extension interface. Vite builds the dashboard, and WXT packages the Chrome extension. The backend is a Hono API running on Cloudflare Workers. It stores records in Cloudflare D1 using Drizzle ORM, and keeps file attachments in Cloudflare R2.

Try it 🔑

Install Global Login from the Chrome Web Store and choose Add to Chrome. The listing is currently unlisted, so use that direct link to find it. I plan to make it public and searchable soon. Once your workspace administrator approves your account, open the extension and sign in with Google.

For a manual install, the Chrome ZIP is also available on GitHub Releases.

The source code and self-hosting guide are available if you’d like to run it for your own team.

If someone joined your team tomorrow, which login would they have to ask you for first? That’s the one I’d start with.

articles.title: Building PaperBridge: An Offline-First Optical UI Skeleton for Elder Care with Kiro
articles.description: This post was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.  Most health-tech tools assume the...
articles.body_html:
This post was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

Most health-tech tools assume the person taking the medication has a smartphone, an account and the patience to tap through an app every morning and evening. In real life, that breaks down fast in elder care. Parents and grandparents do far better with a printed sheet on the fridge and a pen.

On the other hand, snapping a photo of a paper chart and sending it to a Vision LLM creates a worse problem: it is slow, sends private medical data to external servers and risks hallucinating faint or messy pen marks. In medication tracking, guessing a missed dose as "taken" is a safety hazard.

For the Kiroween 2026 hackathon, I built PaperBridge: an open-source, offline-first optical skeleton that turns plain printed paper into a fast, deterministic digital interface, powered by Kiro's full developer workflow.

  • Live Demo (Offline PWA): https://paperbridge-acvw.onrender.com/
  • Main Repo: https://github.com/meenanoolu/paperbridge
  • Kiro Crew App Repo: https://github.com/meenanoolu/paperbridge-care-monitor

Elder Care First: Paper as the UI, AI Only Where It Belongs

PaperBridge separates optical reading from AI reasoning:

  1. Deterministic Optical Core (src/core/): Runs 100% client-side in the browser in 28.5 ms median with zero backend and zero Vision LLM calls. It locates 4 corner fiducials, corrects perspective and classifies every bubble locally.
  2. Honest Uncertainty + Human-in-the-Loop: Ambiguous or faint pen marks are never guessed. They are flagged as unclear and the caregiver can click the bubble to verify it as Filled or Blank. The raw optical scan stays immutable, while a "Manually verified (N)" audit badge is stamped on the result.
  3. Real Caregiver Workflows (src/apps/elder-care/): Caregivers customize the patient name, week start date and medication or habit labels before printing a PDF card (bubble coordinates stay identical so the decoder needs zero changes). Scanning tracks adherence, flags missed doses, saves multi-week trends locally and copies a clean Markdown Doctor Visit Summary in one click.
  4. True Offline Resilience: Packaged as an installable PWA with a service worker precaching the app shell, PDF generator and sample cards, so printing, webcam scanning and saving history work even with Wi-Fi turned off.

Built as a Reusable Skeleton

While Elder Care Bridge is the flagship workflow, PaperBridge is architected as a reusable optical skeleton (src/core/ + src/shell/). Any developer can run npm run create-app <slug> "<Display Name>" to scaffold a brand-new paper-based application (such as clinic intake forms or field checklists) with a valid card layout, pure interpreter, <ScanWorkbench> UI and passing property tests in under a minute.

How Kiro Powered the Build

Instead of using Kiro just for one-off code generation, I used all five pillars of the Kiro workflow:

  • Spec-Driven Development (.kiro/specs/paperbridge/): Every core invariant, accessibility requirement (WCAG 2.2 AA/AAA) and workflow phase was tracked across requirements, design and tasks. That discipline produced 149 passing tests, including fast-check property-based tests that verify decoding guarantees.
  • Steering Docs (.kiro/steering/): Custom steering rules lock down the separation between src/core/ and src/apps/ so new features never weaken optical thresholds or mutate raw scan results.
  • Agent Hooks (.kiro/hooks/): Three automated hooks keep the core invariants, sample generation and UI checks aligned as the codebase evolves.
  • Custom Layout Validator MCP Server (mcp/ + .kiro/settings/mcp.json): When designing a new paper card, LLMs can easily place bubbles too close together or overlap corner fiducials. I built a local MCP server exposing validate_card_layout and list_registered_apps so Kiro validates card geometry deterministically before printing.
  • Kiro Crew App (PaperBridge Care): In Elder Care Bridge, clicking Copy for Kiro Crew copies the verified scan JSON (including the "Manually verified" audit trail). Pasting it into PaperBridge Care inside Kiro Crew launches the care-auditor agent with the adherence-analysis skill to draft a warm, accurate caregiver check-in.

What I Learned

The biggest takeaway from building PaperBridge for Kiroween 2026 was knowing where not to use an LLM. Keeping the optical layer 100% deterministic, local and property-tested made the elder care workflow trustworthy, while using Kiro's specs, MCP validation and Kiro Crew agents turned a single-scan prototype into a complete, extensible platform.

Try the live offline demo at paperbridge-acvw.onrender.com or fork the repo to build your own paper-based app!

articles.title: The Third Cup: Five Elements, One IT Company
articles.description: A Little Chinese Philosophy Over Coffee              An Ordinary Afternoon   The afternoon was...
articles.body_html:
A Little Chinese Philosophy Over Coffee

An Ordinary Afternoon

The afternoon was quiet.

Sunlight came through the front window of the café, falling across the table by the window. It was the best seat in the place, though I had never officially declared it so. Regulars seemed to discover that on their own.

I was wiping down the counter when the bell above the door rang.

A familiar customer walked in, a laptop bag over his shoulder and the unmistakable expression of someone who had spent the entire day in meetings.

“The usual?”

“Please. Something a little stronger today.”

“Rough day?”

He took the seat by the window.

“You have no idea. Product wants everything done yesterday. Development says the requirements keep changing. QA keeps finding problems. Infrastructure says nobody understands how much work deployment actually takes. And the business team just wants to know why we haven't launched yet.”

I started grinding the coffee beans.

“Sounds like a perfectly healthy company.”

He looked up at me.

“Are you joking?”

“Just a little.”

I poured the coffee and placed the cup in front of him.

“Actually, there's an ancient Chinese idea that might help explain what you just described.”

He took a sip.

“Please don't tell me it's another management framework.”

“Not a framework. No slides, either. Just an old way of looking at how things relate to one another.”

I leaned against the counter.

“It's called the Five Elements.”

Five Elements, Not Five Departments

He looked at me with mild suspicion.

“The Five Elements?”

“Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water.”

I counted them off on my fingers.

“In Chinese, we call it Wu Xing. It's an ancient way of understanding relationships and changes in the world. It isn't simply about putting five things next to each other. The interesting part is how they interact.”

He glanced around the café.

“So where have you hidden them? Behind the coffee machine?”

I laughed.

“You can see them right now. Wooden tables, metal equipment, water in your cup, heat from the coffee machine, and the ground beneath this building. You just haven't started charging rent for them.”

He laughed and took another sip.

“Fine. So how does this explain my company?”

“Let's try something. Imagine your IT company has five elements of its own.”

A Little Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water

I picked up a clean cup and slowly turned it in my hand.

“Let's start with Wood.”

Wood grows. It reaches outward, puts out branches, and looks for more room.

“In an IT company, I'd associate Wood with the Product team. Product people decide what the company should build, what users might need, and which direction the product should grow.”

“So Product is the tree?”

“More or less. Though some product roadmaps look more like forests nobody has bothered to trim.”

He laughed.

“That sounds familiar.”

I put the cup back on the counter.

“Next comes Fire.”

Fire brings energy. It spreads, attracts attention, and makes things stand out.

“I'd associate Fire with Business Operations: the business and growth side of the company. They take the value created by the product and bring it to users. They help people discover it, use it, and, ideally, generate revenue.”

“Ideally?”

“Well, running a café has taught me one thing: never calculate tomorrow's revenue before the customers have even walked through the door.”

He laughed.

“Fair enough.”

I picked up the milk pitcher, rinsed it, and turned it upside down on the towel.

“Next is Earth. Earth supports everything. It gives other things somewhere to stand.”

“In an IT company, I'd associate Earth with Infrastructure Operations. Servers, networks, databases, deployment environments, monitoring systems, and everything else that keeps the systems running.”

“So, the people nobody notices until something breaks?”

“Exactly. When everything works, nobody asks how the ground beneath their feet is doing. The moment it disappears, suddenly everyone becomes an infrastructure expert.”

He nearly spilled his coffee laughing.

“That's painfully accurate.”

I picked up the coffee pot.

“Next is Metal. I'd associate Metal with Development.”

“Because developers like hardware?”

“Not quite. Think of Metal as something solid and precise, something that can be shaped into a tool. Developers turn ideas into working systems. They solve technical problems, build structures, and make things actually happen.”

“That's a pretty flattering description of us.”

“Don't get too comfortable. Every element has its problems.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“And Water?”

I glanced at the coffee cup in his hand.

“Water is Testing.”

He looked at me.

“Testing? Why Water?”

“Water flows. It passes through different places, finds gaps, reaches corners, and reveals the shape of the places it touches.”

I paused to refill the coffee pot.

“Testing should do something similar. It shouldn't just execute a checklist and report bugs. It should also help information flow between Product, Development, Business, and Infrastructure. It exposes risks, finds weak spots, and helps everyone see what's actually happening.”

“So QA is the water flowing through the whole company?”

“At least, that's how I see it.”

I put the coffee pot back on the warmer.

“Five elements, five different roles. But they're not five isolated departments.”

They Nourish One Another

He looked down at the notes he'd just typed into his phone.

“Okay. What comes next?”

“Now it gets interesting. In the Five Elements, there's a relationship called generating. Put simply, one element nourishes or supports another.”

I took a napkin and drew five small circles on it.

Wood generates Fire. Fire generates Earth. Earth generates Metal. Metal generates Water. Water generates Wood.


He stared at the napkin.

“That sounds like a rather strange company structure.”

“Give it a moment.”

I pointed to the first circle.

“Product creates value. Business Operations brings that value to the market. When the company makes money, it can invest some of that revenue in infrastructure.”

I moved to the next circle.

“Infrastructure supports Development. Development builds the system. Testing examines it, finds problems, and sends information back to Product.”

“And then Product keeps improving?”

“Exactly. And the cycle starts again.”

He studied the circles in silence for a few seconds.

“So nobody can really work completely independently.”

“At least, not for very long.”

I folded the napkin and slid it across the table.

A company keeps moving because work doesn't stop at the boundaries between departments.

Sometimes, Holding Each Other Back Is Necessary

He finished his coffee and leaned back in his chair.

“But if everyone is supposed to support everyone else, why do companies still argue so much?”

“Because there's another kind of relationship.”

I collected his empty cup and carried it to the sink.

“In Chinese, we call it overcoming. One element places limits on another.”

I rinsed the cup and put it back on the shelf.

“Think about your company. Product can't keep adding features forever. Development can't spend six months pursuing technical perfection for every little feature. Testing can't hold every release indefinitely. Business can't chase growth while ignoring quality. And Infrastructure can't reject every change just because things are stable right now.”

He nodded slowly.

“So sometimes they have to disagree.”

“Of course. A little disagreement can actually make a company healthier.”

I dried my hands.

Overcoming isn't about destroying the other side. It's about preventing one force from growing so much that the whole system can no longer handle it.

He glanced at the napkin again.

“That might be more useful than another team-building workshop.”

“Possibly. And it's cheaper. All you need is a napkin and a cup of coffee.”

There's More to the Story

The sunlight had shifted from one side of the table to the other. His coffee was gone, and he had finally stopped checking his phone every few minutes.

“Is that all there is to the Five Elements?”

I smiled and continued wiping the counter.

“Not even close.”

“I knew it.”

“There's much more to it. The relationships are far more complicated than five names and a circle. Each element has its own characteristics, too. Some things aren't quite as simple as they first appear.”

I glanced toward the window.

“Take Earth, for example. It's a little different from the other four.”

“How so?”

I picked up his empty cup.

That's a story for another cup.

He laughed.

“I'll remember that.”

“Good. I'm running a café. I need regular customers.”

He packed up his laptop and stood.

At the door, he turned around.

“So, which element do you think I am? Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, or Water?”

I pretended to think carefully.

“Today? Probably Water. You've spent the whole week flowing from one meeting to another.”

He shook his head, laughing.

“See you next time.”

“Your seat will be waiting.”

The door closed behind him.

I looked at the napkin he'd left on the table. Five little circles, with a few lines connecting them.

I picked it up, folded it, and placed it beside the coffee machine.

There were plenty of other things we could talk about.

Just not today.

The afternoon was still warm, the coffee was still good, and another customer was already walking toward the door.

P.S. English isn't my first language, so I use AI to help polish my writing and smooth out the rough edges. Thanks for reading.

☕ Buy me a coffee

P.P.S. The paperback edition of my earlier book is now available.

Amazon - AI, Ego & Regret

articles.description: TL;DR: Your green contribution squares are a heatmap. I wanted a chart. So I built...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR: Your green contribution squares are a heatmap. I wanted a chart.
So I built gh-trading-terminal: a GitHub Action that renders your real contribution calendar as a TradingView / Bloomberg-style terminal, as one self-contained SVG you drop into your profile README.

🔗 Repo: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal (MIT, Node 18.3+, 0 dependencies)


The preview uses synthetic sample data. Yours uses your real contribution calendar.

🧭 What's inside the terminal

Every panel is plain SVG, and you choose which ones to show:

Panel What it draws show name
🕯️ Candlesticks One daily candle per day, with a pulsing candle for the current UTC day (always on)
🔊 Volume Raw contributions per day under the chart volume
📊 Analytics 10 stats: total, avg/day, active days, current and longest streak, best day, volatility (σ), Sharpe, max drawdown, best weekday stats
🟩 Heatmap Last 26 weeks, weekday × week heatmap
📈 Weekly volume Last 12 weeks, with week-over-week change weekly
🗓️ Monthly close Last 6 months, with month-over-month change monthly
🧾 Ticker tape A scrolling strip of your key numbers tape
〰️ SMA A 20-period moving average line sma
🌫️ Bands A ±2σ band around the same 20-period window bands

Everything is on by default except bands (use show: all to turn it on).

💡 The header also shows your Developer Index, a fictional 0 to 1000 score, with a sparkline and a pulsing LIVE dot.

⚡ Setup in 3 steps (no server, no hosting)

Step 1: Add a workflow

In your profile repo (USERNAME/USERNAME), create .github/workflows/terminal.yml:

name: Update trading terminal
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: '17 */6 * * *' }]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  terminal:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal@v1
        with:
          days: 90
          theme: tradingview
          token: ${{ secrets.GH_PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

Step 2: Run it once

Go to the Actions tab → Update trading terminal → Run workflow.
It renders and commits two files:

  • assets/terminal-dark.svg
  • assets/terminal-light.svg

Step 3: Embed it in your profile README.md

This <picture> block follows the viewer's light/dark theme:

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="assets/terminal-light.svg">
  <img src="assets/terminal-dark.svg" width="100%" alt="GitHub contribution trading terminal">
</picture>

🔒 Want your private contributions included?
  1. Create a token with the read:user scope.
  2. Save it as the repo secret GH_PAT.
  3. Enable "Private contributions" in your GitHub profile settings.

If the default token is rejected, use GH_PAT. That's why the workflow reads secrets.GH_PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN.

🎛️ Action inputs

input default notes
username repo owner any GitHub login
days 90 14 to 730
theme / light-theme tradingview / light tradingview, bloomberg, midnight, light
output-dir assets where the SVGs are written
show all but bands stats,heatmap,weekly,monthly,volume,tape,sma,bands or all
extra-args (empty) any CLI flag, e.g. --colorblind true --hide tape --up #00ff88
commit true set false to handle commits yourself

🎨 The four themes
Theme Look
tradingview the default dark theme (navy background, teal/red candles)
bloomberg amber text on pure black, green/red candles
midnight GitHub-dark style palette
light the default for terminal-light.svg

♿ Colorblind mode and custom colors

Colorblind mode swaps the candle colors to blue (up) and orange (down):

- uses: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal@v1
  with:
    extra-args: "--colorblind true --hide tape --up #00ff88"

⚠️ Quote the extra-args value. In YAML, an unquoted # starts a comment, so --up #00ff88 would silently get cut off.

Color flags: --up, --down, --bg. The smoothing factor is --alpha (default 0.5, clamped to 0.1 to 0.9).


🧮 How the numbers work

GitHub only exposes daily contribution totals, so real intraday OHLC data does not exist.
Instead, candles are a deterministic mapping of your real counts. Nothing is fabricated.

The "price" is an exponential moving average (EMA) of your daily activity:

level(t) = level(t-1) + alpha * (count(t) - level(t-1))

From that level, each candle is built like this:

open  = level(t-1)
close = level(t)
high  = max(open, close, count(t), count(t-1))
low   = min(open, close, count(t), count(t-1))
  • 🟢 green when close >= open (the day beat the running level)
  • 🔴 red otherwise

A few details I like:

  • Volume is the raw count per day. Huge spikes are clipped to a sensible axis limit and marked with a small triangle, so one monster day can't flatten the whole chart.
  • An empty in-progress day does not break your current streak yet. The day isn't over.
  • The current UTC day is drawn as a pulsing, translucent candle, because that session is still open.

The Developer Index (0 to 1000)

A rolling 28-day blend of four components. It's fictional, but fully reproducible:

Component Weight How it's computed
Active-day ratio 35% share of days in the window with at least 1 contribution
Intensity 25% log(1 + mean) / log(1 + 10), capped at 1
Streak 20% current streak ÷ 14 days, capped at 1
Stability 20% 1 - min(1, stdDev / mean / 3)

Two more stats complete the picture:

  • Sharpe = mean ÷ standard deviation of your daily counts
  • Max drawdown = the worst peak-to-trough fall of the Developer Index

⚠️ It's a joke index with real math behind it. Not financial advice, and not a performance review either.

🧱 The constraint that shaped everything

GitHub serves README images through an image proxy that blocks scripts, CSS and web fonts. So the SVG is built to survive that:

  • ✅ plain SVG attributes only (no <style>, no scripts, no external references)
  • ✅ a system monospace font stack
  • ✅ SMIL for all animation: the pulsing candle, the LIVE dot and the scrolling tape
  • ✅ works in any <img> tag
  • ✅ self-contained: about 38 KB at 90 days, and still under about 100 KB at the 730-day maximum

The test suite even enforces it: every theme is rendered and asserted to contain no <script>, <style>, <foreignObject> or external URLs.

Other things worth knowing:

  • GraphQL allows under a year per query, so longer ranges are chunked automatically (360-day chunks, de-duplicated by date).
  • GitHub caches images, so changes can take a few minutes to show. The SVG prints its own UPDATED time.
  • Commits made by the Action bot don't count as your contributions. (No infinite-green-squares exploit, sorry.)

🛠️ Other ways to run it

CLI (Node 18.3+, zero dependencies):

git clone https://github.com/hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal && cd gh-trading-terminal
npm test
npm run demo        # synthetic data, no token needed
GITHUB_TOKEN=xxx node src/cli.js --user YOU --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-11-22 --theme bloomberg --out terminal.svg

🚩 All CLI flags 
--user --days --from --to --theme --show --hide
--animate false --colorblind true
--up --down --bg --alpha --demo --out

Live URL (optional): deploy to Vercel, set GITHUB_TOKEN, and use this as the image URL (served by api/terminal.js, cached for 1 hour):

https://YOUR-APP.vercel.app/api/terminal?user=YOU&theme=bloomberg&days=120

✅ Tested

npm test runs 6 tests with Node's built-in test runner. They cover candle invariants, streak logic, rendering every theme safely, display toggles and input validation, the chunked GraphQL fetch, and the Action's entrypoint script. CI runs them on Node 18, 20 and 22.

🤝 Contributing

PRs are welcome, and the layout is easy to navigate:

You want to add... Look in
a new theme src/themes.js
layout changes src/render.js
new metrics src/analytics.js

Run npm test before opening a PR.

🎬 Try it

  1. ⭐ Star the repo: hanzlabaig-dev/gh-trading-terminal
  2. Drop the workflow into your profile repo
  3. Tell me in the comments: what's your Developer Index? 📈

Which panel or metric should I add next? Let me know below. 👇

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

DRY STATIC is a dry breath-hold trainer for freedivers that checks each hold with the camera instead of trusting a stopwatch.

Freedivers train on land every day with CO2 and O2 tables: a set of timed holds and rests, done seated or lying down, never in water. Today's table apps are timers. You tap to say the hold started, you tap for your first contraction, you tap when it ends. Nothing checks whether the hold was real, whether you sneaked a breath, or when the involuntary diaphragm contractions began.

DRY STATIC runs the same tables, but it watches the breathing waveform from the SmartSpectra SDK while each hold runs:

  • A hold is verified, not assumed. During a real hold the chest and abdomen traces go flat. Each hold ends as verified, breath detected, or partly readable, with the share of the hold the camera could actually see.
  • Contraction marks (experimental). Diaphragm contractions show up as short jerks in the abdominal trace. The app marks them and scores the marks against your own taps.
  • Pulse only after the hold. The SDK's pulse is a 12-second average, so showing it mid-hold would misstate when it was measured. It appears in the round summary, with the drop across the hold.

There is no dashboard, no streaks and no score. Each round gets a strip chart and at most three plain sentences.

Demo

The video plays the bundled replay (a synthetic recording, labeled as such in the app) at 4x speed, then shows the analyzer output from a real session of three dry holds.

Code

chintandb / dry-static

DRY STATIC

A dry apnea table trainer for freedivers that uses the camera to check each hold.

Freedivers train breath-holds on land with CO2 and O2 tables: a fixed series of timed holds and rests, done seated or lying down. Most table apps are a stopwatch, and nothing checks the hold itself. A small breath, a pause to talk, or a lost camera view all pass unnoticed. DRY STATIC reads the breathing traces from the Presage SmartSpectra SDK and uses them for three things: it checks that each hold stayed still, it marks diaphragm contractions (experimental), and it shows how your pulse changed after each hold.

It is a desktop app built with Electron and TypeScript. It runs on macOS with Apple Silicon and needs Node.js 20 or newer.

Demo video (2:54): docs/demo.mp4. It plays the bundled synthetic recording at 4x speed, then shows the analyzer output from a…

View on GitHub

Try it with no key and no camera:

git clone https://github.com/chintandb/dry-static.git
cd dry-static
npm install
npm run replay   # bundled synthetic recording
npm test         # 186 tests, no camera or key

Live mode: cp .env.example .env, add your PRESAGE_API_KEY, then npm start. macOS arm64.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Signals used: chest breathing trace, abdominal breathing trace, breathing rate, pulse rate, and the talking flag. If the key refuses that set, the app falls back to the three breathing metrics alone. It also listens to the SDK's validation codes and hints.

What happens in real time:

  1. Framing. The SDK's validation hints ("move back", "chest not visible" and so on) are turned into one short instruction. Continue unlocks only after the SDK reports a good view for 3 s and both breathing traces are arriving.
  2. Settle-in, 45 s. The app learns how big your normal breathing is on each trace, picks the cleaner one, and records your resting pulse.
  3. During each hold a status chip updates live:
    • HOLD VERIFIED while the trace stays flat.
    • BREATH DETECTED if the trace moves away from its recent baseline by more than 0.4x your normal breathing size for at least 0.4 s. The baseline is a trailing 12 s median, so a quick exhale-and-sip shows up instead of being averaged away.
    • NOT READABLE when samples stop for more than 1.5 s, the SDK's validation code stays bad for more than 1.5 s, or the SDK reports talking. A hold is never smoothed over.
  4. After each hold: the verdict, your pulse curve and drop, and your breathing rate as it recovers.

Integration. It is an Electron app. The renderer runs the SmartSpectra Node SDK on the camera stream, and the main process holds the API key and the SDK's IPC bridge, so the key never reaches the page. The renderer is sandboxed. Every packet is timestamped on the SDK clock, and taps are mapped onto that clock through a median offset, so marks and taps line up. Telemetry is off. The same detectors run offline over recorded sessions (npm run analyze), which is how they were tested.

What a real session showed. I recorded three real dry holds (27 s, 13 s, 27 s):

Result
Hold verdicts 3 of 3 verified, 98–99.5% of each hold readable, 30 Hz, no gap over 0.03 s
Pulse drop −7.7 and −17.3 BPM (round 1 had no pulse reading before the hold)
Contraction marks vs my taps 0 of 6 matched. My waist was out of frame, so there was no abdominal trace

The first version flagged all three real holds as breaths. Two things from the real data changed the detector:

  • The chest kept settling for 5 to 8 s after the last inhale, so the first 8 s of a hold are now ignored (it was 3 s).
  • A felt contraction moved the chest trace 0.74x my normal breathing size for 1.6 s, which is enough to look like a breath. A short movement (2.5 s or less) next to a contraction tap is now excused, and the round summary lists it instead of hiding it.

The pass/fail thresholds were written before any data. Contraction marks failed them, so they stay labeled experimental.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use.

The need. In apnea training, how long a hold lasted and when contractions started are the main progress markers, and today they are self-reported. A camera that can see a breath makes the training log honest without a chest strap or any extra hardware.

Who it's for. Freedivers and breath-hold trainees doing dry tables at home, seated, with a laptop.

Designed for them:

  • Safety before the camera. Six checks (dry land, seated or lying down, someone nearby, no hyperventilation, stop at the first strong urge) must all be ticked before the camera opens. Holds are capped at 50–60% of your personal best, below the usual top of a classic O2 table, and nothing ever extends a hold. Stop is always one click away.
  • Honest output. Every verdict says how much of the hold was readable. A short movement excused by a contraction tap is still listed. Pulse is never shown during a hold because it lags.
  • Calm interface. One chip, one trace, a big timer. No rankings and no streaks that would push someone to hold longer.
  • Works without a key. Replay mode and the offline analyzer let anyone check the detectors without a camera or a trial.

Consent and Data Handling

Consent. The first screen says what the app does, what the camera is used for, what is stored, and that telemetry is off, before anything opens. The safety screen follows. The camera opens only after both, and only for the length of a session. The app grants camera access (video only, no microphone) to its own bundled page and denies every other permission request.

What is stored. Only numbers: breathing trace values, breathing rate, pulse rate, the talking flag, the SDK's validation codes, and the app's own timings (hold start and end, taps). No video, no images, no face data, and no text are stored.

Where. Everything stays on the Mac, in the app's data folder (~/Library/Application Support/dry-static/data; the About & Data screen shows the exact path): session summaries, recordings of the signal values, and a local count of live minutes used.

Sharing. Nothing is shared. The SmartSpectra SDK processes the camera feed and contacts Presage for authentication and processing; that is the SDK's own traffic. SDK telemetry is switched off (enableTelemetry: false), the app requests no Presage cloud insights, and it uses no AI service and makes no other network requests. There is no account, no analytics and no tracker.

Retention and deletion. Data stays until you delete it. One "Delete all data" button, on History and on About & Data, removes the whole data folder. CSV and PNG exports are written only to a file you choose.

The key. PRESAGE_API_KEY is read from .env or the environment in the main process. It is never logged, never shown, and never written into a recording. .env is git-ignored.

Not a medical device. DRY STATIC is a training aid for dry breath-hold practice. It does not measure oxygen or carbon dioxide, it cannot detect a blackout, and it is not a safety device. Never use it in or near water. People with heart, lung, blood-pressure or seizure conditions, and anyone pregnant, should talk to a doctor before starting breath-hold training. SmartSpectra metrics are for general wellness and informational purposes only and have not been cleared by the FDA.

articles.title: Local AI Code Review Before a PR: Tools That Catch Bugs Before You Push
