articles.title: BadUSB Works Because Trust Was Designed for Convenience, Not Verification
articles.description: Your computer does not ask if the keyboard is lying. It just starts typing.   Plug something...
articles.body_html:
Your computer does not ask if the keyboard is lying. It just starts typing.

Plug something into a USB port and watch what happens. Nothing asks for permission. Nothing asks for proof. The operating system sees a new device, reads a little ID card it hands over, and says, cool, welcome aboard. If that ID card says keyboard, the computer believes it. If it says mouse, it believes that too. If it says storage drive, network adapter, serial port, audio interface, or all five at once, it believes all of it.

That is not a bug that slipped through QA. That is the design. USB was built to make hardware disappear into the background, to make setup feel like magic. You plug it in, it works. No driver hunt, no config file, no interrogation. Convenience was the product. Verification was never invited to the meeting.

BadUSB lives in that gap.

It is not really about a specific stick, a specific brand, or a specific payload. It is about a protocol that trusts first and asks questions never. A BadUSB device is just a microcontroller that has learned to lie fluently in the language of USB descriptors. It tells your machine a story, and your machine, polite to a fault, believes every word.

This is why the attack feels almost unfair. It does not need you to click a sketchy link. It does not need you to disable your antivirus. It does not need a zero day. It just needs three seconds of physical access and a port that is feeling generous, which is to say, any port.

The lie starts before the operating system wakes up

When a USB device connects, it goes through enumeration. Think of it as a very short job interview where the applicant writes their own resume and the interviewer never calls references.

The device presents a vendor ID, a product ID, a device class, and a set of descriptors that say what it claims to be. The host reads them and loads the appropriate driver. A keyboard gets the HID driver. A flash drive gets the mass storage driver. A network adapter gets a network driver.

Here is the part that should make you uncomfortable: those IDs are not verified against a hardware root of trust. They are just numbers the firmware reports. A ten dollar microcontroller can claim to be a keyboard made by a major manufacturer, and Windows, macOS, and Linux will all nod along. There is no cryptographic signature on the claim. There is no challenge. There is no, prove you are who you say you are.

That is the first failure, and it is architectural. We built a universal bus for the entire planet and gave it the security model of a name tag at a conference. Hi, my name is KEYBOARD. Oh, great, come right in.

Once enumeration succeeds, the device is trusted. And trusted, in USB land, means powerful.

A keyboard is a god

People underestimate keyboards because they are boring. They sit there. They clack. They spill coffee. But from the perspective of an operating system, a keyboard is not a peripheral. A keyboard is a user.

When a keyboard sends keystrokes, the OS does not treat them as suggestions from an external gadget. It treats them as intent from the human sitting in front of the screen. That distinction matters enormously. A program trying to open a terminal, download a file, and run it would trigger a dozen alarms. A keyboard doing the exact same thing by typing the exact same commands is just... a person working.

BadUSB exploits that semantic loophole beautifully. It does not inject code through a vulnerability. It injects keystrokes through a trusted channel. It opens Run with Win plus R, types powershell, hits enter, types a one liner that pulls down a second stage, and hits enter again. To the machine, you just did that. To the logs, you just did that. To the security software watching for malicious processes, a human just did that, and humans are allowed to do weird things.

Speed is the other weapon. A BadUSB device can type at inhuman speed, hundreds of characters per second, with perfect accuracy, while also inserting delays exactly where a human would pause. It can wait for the desktop to load. It can wait for a UAC prompt and press the right arrow key. It can adapt. Modern payloads are not dumb scripts. They check the OS, check the keyboard layout, check if a window opened, and branch accordingly. They are tiny robots pretending to be you, and they are very good at it.

And because the attack happens at the HID layer, it bypasses almost everything we normally rely on. Antivirus does not scan keystrokes for malware. EDR does not flag a keyboard for typing too fast, at least not by default. Network firewalls do not care that the command to exfiltrate data was typed rather than downloaded. The whole defensive stack is built on the assumption that input from a keyboard equals input from a legitimate user. BadUSB breaks that assumption, then walks right through the hole.

It is not just keyboards anymore

The classic BadUSB story is the fake keyboard. The modern BadUSB story is much messier.

A single device can enumerate as multiple devices at once. It can be a keyboard and a mouse and a storage drive and a network adapter, all in one tiny package. That composite trick opens up attacks that look even more innocent.

Enumerate as a network adapter, for example, and you can hijack DNS. The computer thinks it just plugged in a new Ethernet dongle, assigns it a route, and starts sending traffic through it. Suddenly the attacker is in the middle, serving fake login pages, intercepting requests, downgrading connections. The user sees nothing. No popup. No warning. Just a slightly slower internet connection for a minute.

Enumerate as storage, and you can serve a fake installer. Enumerate as a serial device, and you can talk to internal tools that assume serial means local and safe. Enumerate as a mouse, and you can move the cursor, click through prompts, approve things the user never approved. The mouse does not need permission to click Allow. The mouse is allowed to click Allow. That is its job.

Even scarier, BadUSB devices can reprogram themselves on the fly. A drive that looks like boring storage when you first plug it in can flip to keyboard mode after a delay, or after it detects a specific OS, or after it receives a trigger. Firmware is software. Software can lie, wait, and change its story. The device you inspected five minutes ago is not necessarily the device you are plugged into now.

This is why the old advice, just do not plug in random USB drives, is both correct and completely insufficient. It assumes the threat is the drive you found in the parking lot. The real threat is any USB device whose firmware you do not control, which is to say, almost every USB device you own.

Why we cannot just patch this away

If BadUSB is so simple, why has it not been fixed in twenty years? Because fixing it would break the thing people actually love about USB: it just works.

Real verification would mean every USB device needs a cryptographic identity, every OS needs to check that identity against a trusted registry, and every user needs to approve new devices in a way that cannot be spoofed by a fake keyboard. That is doable in theory. It is miserable in practice.

Imagine plugging in a new mouse and getting a prompt that says, do you trust this mouse? Most people would click yes without reading. Then the fake keyboard would just type yes for them. Or it would wait until you approve a legitimate device, then piggyback on that approval. Human approval is a weak gate when the attacker controls an input device that can simulate human approval.

There are defenses, and they are worth using. USB device allowlisting, kernel level HID filtering, disabling USB ports in BIOS, using USB data blockers that only pass power, requiring physical presence for new devices, endpoint tools that alert on new HID devices appearing out of nowhere. All of them help. None of them are default. None of them are frictionless. And friction is exactly what USB was designed to eliminate.

Corporations can enforce strict policies. They can glue ports shut. They can deploy allowlists. They can train staff. Home users, small labs, makers, students, and everyone else living in the real world cannot realistically do that for every charger, every dongle, every borrowed cable, every conference swag stick.

So we live with the tradeoff. We chose convenience. We got convenience. We also got a universal attack surface shaped exactly like convenience.

The social engineering is the port itself

BadUSB is often framed as a hardware hack. It is better understood as a social hack that happens to use hardware.

The attack works because we have trained people, for decades, to trust ports. Plug in to charge. Plug in to present. Plug in to transfer photos. Plug in to use the printer. The port is a helpful hole in the side of the machine. It is not coded in our brains as a threat.

Attackers know this. That is why BadUSB payloads show up disguised as things people want to plug in: a free phone charger at an airport, a branded USB drive at a trade show, a replacement cable that looks identical to the real one, a promotional gadget that promises to speed up your computer. The device does not need to be found. It needs to be wanted.

Even without malice, the ecosystem is leaky. Cheap cables with hidden chips exist. Counterfeit devices with reprogrammable firmware exist. Supply chain tampering exists. You do not need a nation state actor to get a BadUSB device. You need an internet connection, a microcontroller, and a weekend. The barrier to entry is low, the payoff is high, and the victim often never knows what happened.

That asymmetry is the point. The defender has to secure every port, every device, every user, every time. The attacker has to get one device plugged in once.

What actually helps, if you are honest about it

Let us skip the fantasy advice. No one is going to stop using USB. No one is going to manually audit every descriptor of every device they own. So what moves the needle?

First, treat USB like network access, because that is what it is. A USB port is not a power outlet. It is a network interface that can pretend to be a user. If you would not plug an unknown Ethernet cable into your laptop, do not plug in an unknown USB device either. Same logic, same risk.

Second, separate charging from data. If you just need power, use a charge only cable or a USB data blocker. It is a dumb little adapter that cuts the data lines and only passes power. It turns a potentially hostile port into a dumb battery. Keep one in your bag. It is the cheapest security upgrade you will ever buy.

Third, assume any device that can type can own you. That means no borrowing keyboards at events, no plugging in that cool gadget your friend just built without checking it in a lab VM first, no using the free charging station that also wants to sync your phone. If a device enumerates as HID, it has the keys to the kingdom. Treat it accordingly.

Fourth, if you run a lab or a workspace, use allowlisting. It is annoying to set up, but it is the only defense that actually addresses enumeration. Only approved vendor and product IDs get to load drivers. Everything else gets blocked and logged. Pair that with alerts for new HID devices, and you at least get a signal when something weird shows up.

Fifth, practice the boring stuff. Lock your screen when you walk away. Disable autorun. Keep your OS patched, because BadUSB often chains into a second stage that does rely on a software bug. Use a separate, isolated machine or VM for testing unknown hardware. Never test a suspicious device on your main machine with your real accounts logged in. That is not paranoia. That is lab hygiene.

And finally, learn how the attack works by building it in a controlled lab, on your own hardware, with your own payloads, against machines you own. There is no better way to understand trust than to break it yourself, safely, and watch how easily a machine obeys a fake keyboard. Reading about BadUSB is interesting. Watching your own test laptop open a shell because a tiny board told it to is educational in a way no blog post can match.

Convenience was a choice, and we are still paying for it

BadUSB is not going away because the conditions that created it are not going away. We want devices that work instantly. We want ports that accept anything. We want zero friction. Vendors want to sell hardware that works everywhere. Operating systems want to be helpful. Users want to plug and play.

All of those wants are reasonable. All of them together create a system where identity is asserted, never proven, and where a keyboard is trusted absolutely because we never imagined a keyboard would lie.

The fix is not a single patch or a single product. It is a shift in mental model. Stop thinking of USB as a cable. Start thinking of it as a trust decision. Every time something goes into that port, you are making a decision about what you will allow to act as you, to see your network, to touch your files. That decision deserves a second of thought, even if the port was designed to make you skip it.

Your computer trusts too easily because we told it to. BadUSB just takes us at our word.

Further reading from numbpilled

If you want to go from understanding BadUSB to practicing it safely in your own lab, these guides go deep on authorized hardware testing, payload structure, and defensive setup:

Flipper Zero Black Book: 37 Flipper Zero techniques across BadUSB, NFC/RFID, Sub-GHz and BLE/Wi-Fi/GPIO

Flipper Zero Lab Manual: 37 Authorized Hardware Workflows

Vault Pass: 214-Product Numbpilled Archive Snapshot

AI Red Team Archive: LLM Security, Cloud Escalation and Defensive Testing

Hardware Lab Archive: RF, UART, Firmware and Cyberdeck Builds

All guides are for authorized use only: your own devices, data, and systems you have permission to test.

Follow for more field notes on hardware, OSINT, and defensive security: numbpilled.gumroad.com

articles.title: His Green Squares
articles.description: MONDAY: HIS   Kabir's profile is the first thing I see when I open my laptop on Monday...
articles.body_html:
MONDAY: HIS

Kabir's profile is the first thing I see when I open my laptop on Monday morning, because I left his tab open on Friday and never closed it. Forty-one weeks. A solid wall of green, no gaps, not one grey square in the whole row. The darkest green is the kind you get from twenty commits in a day. He has squares that dark in March, in July, in a week I know for a fact he was on holiday, because he sent me a photo of a beach and I replied with the thumbs-up emoji like a person who had never envied anyone in his life.

I scroll down to my own profile. My wall has a hole in it shaped like last Wednesday, when I spent the whole day reading a log file and changed nothing, and another hole shaped like the weekend, when I was not at my laptop at all. My green is the pale kind. Two commits, three commits, the colour of someone who showed up and did a normal amount of work.

Kabir walks past my desk with his coffee and asks what I'm working on. I tell him. He nods in the way people nod when they already knew the answer and asked anyway to be polite.

MONDAY: MINE

My Monday is a bug I cannot reproduce. It happens on the customer's machine and nowhere else. I spend four hours adding logging to a function I am fairly sure is innocent, and then I spend another hour staring at the logs it produces, which say the function is innocent. I commit nothing. There is nothing to commit. "Added logging, learned nothing" is not a commit message you push to a shared branch unless you want a conversation about it in standup.

At 6:40 I close the laptop. My square for today is grey. It will stay grey.

TUESDAY: HIS

Kabir commits at 09:12, 09:47, 10:03, 11:20, and 13:58. I know this because his graph updates while I am waiting for a build. Five commits before lunch. I have made one, and it is a comment I added to my own code because future me kept misunderstanding it, and I am not sure that counts as work even though it took twenty minutes to write the comment properly.

In the afternoon he pushes a fix with the message "typo". Then another one, also "typo". I open the second one. He changed "recieve" to "receive" in a readme. The commit is real. The diff is one word. The square is green either way.

TUESDAY: MINE

The bug reproduces. Once. At 11:04, on the customer's machine, while I am watching over a screen share, it happens exactly once and then never again. The customer laughs. I do not laugh. I write down the exact time, the exact click order, the exact version number, like a person taking notes at a crime scene where the criminal has already left.

I find it at 16:20. It is a race condition, two things finishing in the wrong order, and it only happens when the network is slow in one very specific way. The fix is eleven lines. I test it six times. It holds. I push at 17:02 with a message that says what the bug was and how the fix works, because the next person to read this code deserves to know. One commit. One pale green square. The best day of work I have had in a month, and the graph will never know the difference between this and the typo.

WEDNESDAY: HIS

Kabir is not at his desk. His status says "focus time" and his graph says he has already committed twice today, both before 9 a.m.

At lunch someone asks him how he stays so consistent. He shrugs and says he just commits every day. He says it the way people say they just run every morning, as if the sentence itself were the whole explanation. Nobody asks what the commits contain. I don't ask either. I am too busy deciding whether I am angry at him or at myself, and the answer is myself, and I hate that the answer is myself.

WEDNESDAY: MINE

I spend Wednesday in a design review for a feature that will not be built for three months. I say useful things. I draw a diagram on the whiteboard that three people photograph. I write no code. My square is grey by 3 p.m. and I know it will stay grey, and I catch myself thinking about whether I could push something small tonight, just to fill it, just so the week doesn't have a hole in it.

I could. I have a branch with a half-finished cleanup in it. I could push the half-finished cleanup. It would be green. It would also be a half-finished cleanup on the shared branch at 11 p.m., which is the kind of thing you do when the graph matters more than the code, and I sit there for a full minute with my hand on the laptop, deciding which one matters more to me.

I don't push it. I close the laptop and go home. The grey square stays grey.

THURSDAY: HIS

Kabir's wall hits forty-two weeks. Someone in the team chat posts a screenshot of it with a fire emoji. Three people react with the same emoji. Kabir replies with the folded-hands emoji, which is the correct reply, the humble reply, the reply of a man who did not ask for a screenshot of his graph to be posted in the team chat and also did not ask for it not to be.

I look at his graph again. Forty-two weeks, no gaps. I count the dark green squares. There are eleven of them. Eleven days with twenty or more commits. I think about what twenty commits in a day actually looks like, and the picture in my head is not a person doing twenty pieces of work. I don't know which one it is. I have never asked. Asking would sound like an accusation, and I am not sure it isn't one.

THURSDAY: MINE

The race-condition fix breaks something else. Of course it does. The thing it breaks is a report that nobody has looked at in six weeks, and it breaks it in a way that only shows up when the report is run on a Thursday, which is today. I find out at 10:15 from a message that starts "hey, quick question" and ends with a screenshot of numbers that are wrong in a way I recognise immediately, because I am the person who made them wrong yesterday.

I spend the day unbreaking it. The fix for the fix is four lines and a test that would have caught both bugs, the first one and the second one, if I had written it on Tuesday. I write it on Thursday instead. I push at 18:40. One commit. Pale green. The graph records a normal day.

FRIDAY: HIS

Kabir leaves early. He has a flight. His graph for today is already green, two commits before noon, and I know without checking that one of them says "typo" and the other one says "wip". Work in progress. A commit called "wip" is a square like any other. The wall does not ask what the work was.

FRIDAY: MINE

On Friday afternoon I deploy the race-condition fix for real. It goes out with the Thursday test and the four-line repair, and the customer's machine stops doing the thing it did once at 11:04 on Tuesday. The customer writes back, one line: "looks good, thanks". I read that line three times. It is the best code review I have had all week.

Then I do something I have not done in months. I open my own profile and look at my graph the way I have been looking at his. My wall has holes in it. Wednesday is grey. Last weekend is grey. The weekend before that is grey too. The green that is there is pale, two commits, three commits, one commit on Tuesday that mattered more than any five-commit day Kabir has had all month, and the graph cannot tell, and it will never be able to tell, because the graph was never measuring the work. It was measuring the pushing.

I scroll back up to Kabir's wall. Forty-two weeks. Solid green. And for the first time all week, I don't envy it. I can see it now for what it is: a man who never missed a day of pushing something, anything, to keep a wall green. Maybe his work is brilliant and the wall is just a side effect. Maybe the wall is the work. I don't know. I have never asked, and I am not going to ask, because the answer would tell me about him and nothing about me.

My square for today is green. One commit, the deploy, the one that mattered. Next to it, Wednesday sits grey, a hole in the wall shaped like a day I spent thinking instead of pushing. I look at it for a while. Then I close the tab, and I leave it grey, and I go home.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Mingle (MIT): Bring Your Local Coding Agents into Slack, Discord, Telegram & More — With Zero Servers
articles.description: Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom...
articles.body_html:
Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom tooling is pretty common now. What still bothered me about most agent-to-IM bridges was the cloud relay: if a third-party server sits between your chat apps and your agent, your private work conversations pass through someone else's infrastructure—bringing both the risk of a server breach and the risk of your data being logged or sold.

So I built Mingle (MIT-licensed)—a zero-server desktop app that lets you bring your local coding agents directly into the chat apps you already use: Slack, Discord, Telegram, iMessage, WeChat, Feishu/Lark, WeCom, DingTalk, QQ, and GitHub Issues/PRs.

Why zero-server matters

Mingle has no backend service at all:

  • No Mingle server, no accounts, no telemetry.
  • Direct platform connections: connects straight to each chat platform's official bot interface (or your local Apple ID for iMessage)—never routed through a hosted Mingle relay.
  • Localhost-only surface: the local console and API bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
  • OS keychain for secrets: bot tokens and credentials stay inside macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, or Linux Secret Service.
  • Plain-file memory: each agent's persona and memory are ordinary files in a local folder (ROLE.md, MEMORY.md, and notes/).
  • Optional 24/7 mode on your own hardware: if you want your agent online when your laptop sleeps, you can deploy the runtime to your own SSH host directly from the app—still your machine, no middleman.

What makes it usable in real chats

Connecting a CLI agent to a webhook is easy to demo; making it behave well in daily group chats took most of the real engineering:

  1. One agent, unified memory across chat apps The same agent can join your Slack workspace, Discord server, and Telegram/WeChat groups while sharing one continuous memory. You can ask it in one app what was decided in another, or ask it to forward a summary across platforms.
  2. Parallel side tasks without blocking chat When you hand it heavy work—writing code, investigating a bug, running long shell commands—it forks the work into a background task (opening native threads in Slack, Discord, and Feishu) while staying responsive in the main room.
  3. Group-chat etiquette It listens passively, responds when addressed by name or nickname without needing an @ on every message, and automatically throttles itself in busy channels instead of spamming every turn.
  4. 14 coding-agent harnesses + one-click session handoff Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Cursor, and 9 more harnesses via OAR. You can also hand off an existing session's context and preferences into a Mingle agent in one click.

Honest current status

Mingle started about a week ago and is currently at v0.4.8—definitely early:

  • End-to-end verified harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Kimi Code.
  • Chat platforms: Feishu is battle-tested on a live tenant; the other connectors are currently verified against platform APIs and automated tests.
  • Installers: macOS (Apple-signed & notarized), Windows (unsigned for now), Linux, plus a one-line install script.

Links

  • GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/earayu/Mingle
  • Website & docs: https://mingle.build

If you try it out, I'd love feedback on the zero-server architecture, the SSH deployment flow, or any quirks you hit with a specific chat platform—feel free to drop a comment here or open an issue on GitHub.

articles.title: NFC and RFID Feel Like Magic Because We Hid the Protocol From Users
articles.description: You tap a card. A door opens. A payment clears. Nothing visibly happens in between, and that...
articles.body_html:
You tap a card. A door opens. A payment clears. Nothing visibly happens in between, and that is exactly the point.

You have done it a thousand times. You hold your phone near a terminal, you feel the little buzz, you see the checkmark, you walk away like you just performed a minor miracle. You tap your badge to get into work. You tap your transit card to get on the train. You tap your hotel key to get into a room that, ten seconds earlier, did not know you existed.

It feels like magic because it was designed to feel like magic.

Underneath that tap is a negotiation so fast, so fussy, so paranoid about timing, that if you could hear it, it would sound less like a spell and more like two very nervous robots shouting passwords at each other in a language made of magnetic fields. The reason you do not hear it is not because it is simple. It is because an entire industry spent decades burying the complexity so you would never have to think about it.

And that burial worked a little too well.

We now live in a world where most people think NFC is just “tap to pay,” RFID is just “the thing that beeps at the store exit,” and both are basically Bluetooth but lazier. They are not. They are older, weirder, more physical, and in some ways more honest than almost any other wireless tech you use every day. NFC and RFID do not pretend distance does not matter. They embrace it. They only work when you are close, and that closeness is the security model, the user interface, and the magic trick all at once.

Let us pull the curtain back.

The tap is a handshake, not a wave

When you tap, you are not waving data through the air like Wi-Fi. You are creating a tiny, temporary power plant.

Most RFID and NFC systems work on inductive coupling. That is a fancy way of saying: one coil makes a magnetic field, another coil sits inside that field and steals just enough energy from it to wake up and talk back.

The reader is the loud one. It is constantly shouting into the void: “Anyone there? Anyone there? Anyone there?” in the form of a 13.56 MHz field for NFC and high-frequency RFID, or a lower frequency field for low-frequency tags, or a UHF field for the long-range stuff you see in warehouses.

The tag is the quiet one. Most passive tags have no battery at all. They are dead until they enter the field. Then, for a fraction of a second, they come alive. They harvest power from the reader, boot up a tiny chip, modulate that same field to send back an ID, and then go back to being a piece of plastic.

Think about how absurd that is. Your transit card is a computer with no power source that only exists when you need it. Your office badge is a zombie that wakes up when it gets close to its master. Your hotel key is a secret that only speaks when whispered to by the right lock.

NFC is the chatty cousin in this family. Where basic RFID is often one-way, a tag yelling its ID at a reader, NFC is designed for two-way conversation. Phone to terminal. Phone to phone. Phone to tag. It can read, it can write, it can emulate a card, it can do peer-to-peer. That is why your phone can both pay for coffee and read a smart poster and act like a transit card. It is playing three different roles with the same antenna, and it switches roles so fast you never notice.

The whole transaction, from field to wake to challenge to response to “approved,” happens in under half a second. Your brain interprets that speed as effortlessness. Engineers interpret it as a miracle of timing, because if either side is a millisecond late, the whole thing collapses.

We hid the protocol because the protocol is ugly

Here is the dirty secret of NFC and RFID: the user experience is clean because the protocol is not.

Underneath that tap is a stack of standards with names that sound like they were generated by a committee that hated joy: ISO 14443, ISO 15693, ISO 18092, MIFARE Classic, MIFARE DESFire, FeliCa, NTAG, ICODE. Each one has its own anti-collision rules, its own modulation scheme, its own way of saying “hey, there are two tags here, who goes first,” its own crypto, or lack of crypto, and its own hilarious legacy bugs.

MIFARE Classic, for example, is still everywhere. It is in hotel keys, transit systems, office badges, student IDs, gym memberships. It is also famously broken in ways that security researchers have been writing about since 2007. Its crypto can be cracked. Its keys can be recovered. Its sectors can be cloned if you know what you are doing and you have the right reader and you have permission to test your own cards.

And yet it persists. Why? Because it works. Because it is cheap. Because replacing every reader in every building on earth is expensive. Because “good enough for a gym locker” became “good enough for everything” and nobody wanted to be the person who told a university they had to reissue 40,000 student IDs.

This is the pattern with RFID. The protocol gets hidden not just from users, but from decision makers. A facilities manager does not buy “ISO 14443-A with MIFARE Classic 1K and a known key recovery attack.” They buy “tap badges that open doors.” A hotel chain does not buy “a system with no mutual authentication and predictable UIDs.” They buy “key cards that just work.”

The abstraction is so successful that when something goes wrong, people assume it is magic failing, not engineering failing. “My card stopped working” is rarely about magic. It is about a desynchronized counter, a damaged antenna, a reader that lost power, a tag that got demagnetized by sitting next to a magnet, or a system that was never designed to handle the edge case you just hit.

When you hide the protocol, you also hide the failure modes. And when you hide the failure modes, you create a false sense of security.

Close does not mean safe

The most seductive lie in NFC and RFID is this: because you have to be close, it must be safe.

Closeness helps. It really does. An attacker cannot sniff your NFC payment from across the street the way they could sniff an open Wi-Fi network. They have to be near you, with an antenna, at the exact moment you tap. That raises the bar.

It does not make the bar unreachable.

Proximity is not authentication. Proximity is just proximity. A tag that will talk to any reader that powers it is not verifying identity, it is just being polite. A reader that will accept any UID is not checking a credential, it is checking a serial number that can be copied.

That is why relay attacks work. That is why cloning works. That is why researchers keep demonstrating, year after year, that they can capture a tap, replay it, extend it, or trick a reader into thinking a tag is closer than it is. The attack does not break physics. It abuses trust. It says: “What if I am the reader? What if I am the tag? What if I am just a very long, very invisible wire between the two?”

Modern payment systems know this, which is why they do not just send your card number. Apple Pay and Google Pay do not send your real card number over NFC. They send a token, a one-time cryptogram, a transaction-specific blob that is useless if you steal it and try to reuse it later. That is the difference between a dumb UID and a real secure element doing real cryptography in real time.

Your office badge probably does not do that. Your hotel key probably does not do that. Your gym tag definitely does not do that. They are still playing the old game: “If you know my number, you are me.”

And the number is not secret. It is broadcast to anyone who asks nicely with a magnetic field.

This is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to understand the threat model. The question is never “is RFID secure?” The question is “secure against what, for what asset, for how long?” A $2 tag protecting a $20 locker is a different problem than a $2 tag protecting a data center. A transit card that can be cloned for a free ride is a different problem than a passport that can be skimmed in a crowd.

But when we hide the protocol, we also hide that conversation. Users assume all taps are equal. They are not. Some taps are a cryptographic handshake with a secure element. Some taps are a glorified barcode that happens to be invisible.

Why your phone made it worse, and better

Your phone ruined NFC in the best possible way.

Before smartphones, NFC was mostly a card thing. You had a card, you tapped it, done. The card did one job. It was dumb on purpose.

Then phones got NFC antennas, secure elements, host card emulation, and suddenly your phone could be ten cards at once. It could be your bank card, your transit card, your hotel key, your office badge, your loyalty card, your car key. It could also be a reader. It could read tags, write tags, clone your own tags for backup, emulate tags for testing.

That flexibility is incredible. It is also confusing, because now the same gesture, the same tap, can mean ten different protocols, ten different security levels, ten different failure modes.

You tap to pay and it fails? Is it the terminal? Is it your bank? Is it the token? Is it the antenna alignment? Is it because you have three cards in your wallet and your phone is trying to read all of them at once and getting confused by anti-collision?

You tap to open a door with your phone and it works, but your physical badge does not? Is it because the phone is emulating a different UID? Is it because the reader expects a different application identifier? Is it because the system was configured for cards, not phones, and nobody updated it?

The phone turned NFC from a single-purpose tool into a platform. Platforms are powerful. Platforms are also messy. And because the phone hides all of that mess behind a checkmark and a buzz, you never learn the difference between “NFC failed” and “the application on top of NFC failed.”

That is why troubleshooting NFC feels like voodoo. Hold it a little higher. Hold it a little lower. Take off the case. Turn it off and on again. Move it slowly. Move it fast. Sacrifice a goat. None of that is in the manual, because the manual assumes the protocol will just work. When it does not, you are left with folk magic to fix actual magic.

The real magic is not the tap, it is the agreement

Here is what actually makes NFC and RFID feel like magic: everyone agreed to pretend.

Reader makers agreed to use the same frequencies. Card makers agreed to use the same modulation. Phone makers agreed to support the same standards. Banks agreed to use tokenization. Transit agencies agreed to use the same application IDs. Hotels agreed to use the same key formats, even when those formats were insecure.

That agreement is invisible, but it is the whole trick. Without it, your phone would tap a terminal and get silence. Your badge would tap a reader and get a confused blink. Your transit card would tap a gate and get nothing.

We call it interoperability. It took decades of standards meetings, patent fights, competing formats, and at least one format war that most people never heard about. FeliCa in Japan. MIFARE in Europe. Different frequencies for different uses. Different regulations for different countries. Different power limits. Different antenna sizes.

The fact that you can land in Tokyo with an iPhone and tap your way onto a train, then land in London and tap your way onto the Tube, then land in New York and tap your way into a coffee shop, is not a natural law. It is a negotiated peace treaty between industries that usually hate each other.

And like any peace treaty, it has holes. It has legacy exceptions. It has “we will support this old broken thing because too many people still use it” clauses. It has “this system is secure enough for now” compromises.

The magic is not that the technology is perfect. The magic is that it works at all, despite being built on top of compromises that would make a security auditor cry.

So what do you do with this knowledge?

You do not need to become an RFID engineer to survive in a tap-to-everything world. But you do need to stop thinking of the tap as magic, and start thinking of it as a conversation.

First, assume every tap is a negotiation, not a blessing. If a system will accept any tag that talks to it, it is not verifying you. It is verifying that you have a thing that talks. That might be fine for a loyalty card. It is not fine for a server room.

Second, treat UID as an identifier, not a secret. Your card’s UID is like your username. It is not your password. If a system treats it like a password, that system has a design flaw, not a user flaw.

Third, respect the physical layer. NFC and RFID are physical in a way Wi-Fi is not. Antenna alignment matters. Metal matters. Interference matters. A tag stuck to a metal door will behave differently than a tag stuck to a plastic door. A phone in a thick metal case will behave differently than a phone with no case. You are not doing it wrong. You are fighting physics, and physics does not care about your user experience.

Fourth, if you are building or buying systems, ask the protocol question out loud. What standard is this? What crypto, if any? Does it do mutual authentication? Does it use rolling codes or one-time cryptograms? Can the credential be cloned, and if so, what does cloning get an attacker? How do you revoke it? Those questions sound paranoid until you are the person who has to reissue 5,000 badges because someone cloned one and posted a tutorial.

Fifth, if you are curious, test your own stuff. Legally. On your own cards, your own readers, your own systems, with permission. That is the only way the abstraction stops being scary. Read your own hotel key. See what is actually on it. Read your own transit card. See how much it reveals. Read your own office badge, if your employer allows it, and see if it is just a UID or if there is real crypto underneath.

You will be surprised how often the answer is “just a UID.” And once you see that, you will never look at a tap the same way again.

The protocol was hidden for a reason, but it does not have to stay hidden

There is a good reason we hid the protocol from users. Most people do not want to think about anti-collision algorithms while they are trying to buy coffee. They want coffee. They want the door to open. They want the train to let them through. Good design hides complexity.

Bad design hides consequences.

NFC and RFID sit exactly on that line. They hide complexity beautifully. They hide consequences terribly. They make it easy to use a credential without understanding what that credential actually proves. They make it easy to deploy a system without understanding what that system actually trusts.

The fix is not to make everyone learn ISO 14443 by heart. The fix is to make the abstraction honest. A tap that is just an ID should feel different from a tap that is a cryptographic proof. A system that can be cloned should be labeled as such. A reader that will talk to anything should not pretend it is verifying identity.

Until that happens, the magic will keep working, and the protocol will keep hiding, and most people will keep assuming that because it is fast and close and buzzes nicely, it must be safe.

It is not safe because it is close. It is useful because it is close. Those are different things.

The next time you tap, pause for half a second before you walk away. Feel the buzz. Imagine the field waking up a dead chip. Imagine the chip shouting its secrets to a reader that may or may not deserve them. Imagine the reader deciding, in milliseconds, whether to trust you.

That is not magic. That is engineering, standards, compromises, and a lot of very clever people figuring out how to make invisible conversations feel effortless.

And honestly? That is cooler than magic. Magic does not have to work twice. This does, thousands of times a day, in pockets and wallets and phones all over the world, even when we have no idea how it works.

We hid the protocol to make it feel like magic. Now that you know it is not magic, you get to use it better.

Authorized use only: your own devices, data, and systems you have permission to test.

articles.title: Three date bugs in a 10-line age calculator (and the TZ= trick that exposes them)
articles.description: Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the...
articles.body_html:
Age calculators look like a beginner exercise. Subtract the years, subtract the months, subtract the days, borrow when something goes negative. Mine had all of that. It still told a user born on 31 January that on 1 March they were 26 years, 1 month and −2 days old. On their birthday it said their next birthday was 365 days away.

Here are the three bugs and how I fixed them. If you've ever written new Date(input.value), at least one of them is probably in your code too.

Bug 1: new Date("2026-05-15") is not 15 May in your time zone

An <input type="date"> gives you a string like "2026-05-15". Passing that to new Date() creates midnight UTC, not local midnight. That's ECMAScript's rule for date-only ISO strings.

Then the code calls getDate(), getMonth() and so on, which read local time. In Pakistan (UTC+5) that UTC midnight is 05:00 on the same day, so the date looks right. But:

const nb = new Date(b.getFullYear(), a.getMonth(), a.getDate()); // local midnight
if (nb < b) nb.setFullYear(b.getFullYear() + 1);

On the birthday, nb is 00:00 local and b is 05:00 local, so nb < b is true and the next birthday jumps a year ahead. Hence "365 days".

In US time zones it's worse. UTC midnight is still the previous day locally, so every result was off by a day. The same inputs gave "1 month −2 days" in Lahore and "0 months 29 days" in Los Angeles.

Fix: parse the string yourself as a local calendar date.

function pd(v) {
  const [y, m, d] = v.split('-').map(Number);
  return new Date(y, m - 1, d);       // local midnight
}

The same trap applies the other way. input.valueAsDate = new Date() sets the field to today in UTC, which shows yesterday's date for anyone ahead of UTC just after midnight. Build the YYYY-MM-DD string from the local getFullYear/getMonth/getDate instead.

Bug 2: borrowing days from the wrong month

The classic algorithm:

let d = b.getDate() - a.getDate();
if (d < 0) {
  mo--;
  d += new Date(b.getFullYear(), b.getMonth(), 0).getDate(); // days in previous month
}

Born 31 Jan, today is 1 March: d = 1 - 31 = -30. Borrow February's 28 days and you get −2. The borrow assumes the previous month is long enough to absorb the difference, and February isn't.

Bug 3: there's no single "right" way to borrow, so define one

What is 31 January + 1 month? There's no 31 February. You have to choose, and the common choice (it's what most date libraries do) is to clamp to the last day of the month: 31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb, or 29 in a leap year.

Once you've chosen, the cleanest algorithm doesn't borrow at all. Count whole months, then count the leftover days:

function addMonths(t, n) {
  const y = t.getFullYear(), m = t.getMonth() + n;
  const last = new Date(y, m + 1, 0).getDate();          // last day of target month
  return new Date(y, m, Math.min(t.getDate(), last));     // clamp
}
function dayDiff(x, y) {                                   // DST-safe
  return Math.round((Date.UTC(y.getFullYear(), y.getMonth(), y.getDate())
                   - Date.UTC(x.getFullYear(), x.getMonth(), x.getDate())) / 864e5);
}
function age(a, b) {
  let months = (b.getFullYear() - a.getFullYear()) * 12 + (b.getMonth() - a.getMonth());
  if (addMonths(a, months) > b) months--;                  // this month's anniversary not reached
  const days = dayDiff(addMonths(a, months), b);
  return { years: Math.floor(months / 12), months: months % 12, days };
}

Days can never be negative now, because they're measured forward from the last whole-month anniversary. 31 Jan → 1 Mar is 1 month (to 28 Feb) plus 1 day.

The next birthday falls out of the same helper: addMonths(dob, 12 * yearsSince). That also handles 29 February birthdays (celebrated on the 28th in non-leap years).

How I tested it

  • Edge cases: month ends, 29 Feb in leap and non-leap years, the birthday itself, 31 Dec → 1 Jan.
  • Three time zones: each case ran under TZ=Asia/Karachi, TZ=America/Los_Angeles and TZ=UTC in Node. All three now print identical results. The old code gave a different answer in each zone I tried.
  • 20,000 random date pairs: asserting that days are never negative and months stay within 0–11.

The TZ= trick is the takeaway. If your date code gives different answers when you change the time zone of the machine running it, you have a bug, even if it looks fine where you live.

The calculator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. People mostly use it to check job and admission age limits "as on" a closing date, where being one day off actually matters.

articles.title: My pulse peaked when the practice tower cleared me to land
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge  My pulse climbed most when a...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

My pulse climbed most when a practice tower cleared me to land. The take-off clearance was not far behind.

I was at my desk with a headset on, talking to a simulated tower while the camera followed my pulse. Nothing was moving. Still, it was as if I could really see myself taking off, and then landing.

Both are short messages. The taxi clearance at the start is much longer: a runway, a QNH, a holding point and a route, to read back in order. In that session, my pulse didn't follow the length of the message. It followed what the words meant.

In October I built a practice tower for a friend who is shy about speaking English on the radio. It talks, it listens, and it says "negative" when the QNH is wrong. This month I pointed a camera at the person talking to it.

What I Built

Readback is a radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, and you read back out loud. Meanwhile, the camera follows your pulse and your breathing with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK.

Talking to the tower is one of the things that scare people when they learn to fly. You know the phraseology at home. Then a controller reads you a clearance in one breath, and you have to say it back, in order, while the frequency waits.

A session goes like this:

  1. A consent screen comes first. It says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage, and how to stop.
  2. A calm minute. You sit the way you will for the radio and breathe normally. That minute becomes your reference, for this session only.
  3. A circuit at Isola, a made-up aerodrome: taxi, take-off, a touch and go, a full stop. You hold the space bar to talk. The runway, the QNH and the wind change every game, and a wrong readback gets "negative".
  4. On the side, your pulse and your breathing, shown as differences from your calm minute.
  5. A breathing guide, if your breathing picked up while you listened. It offers three slow breaths before your readback. The tower waits.
  6. A timeline after the circuit. It puts first the messages after which your pulse climbed most.

It's a mirror for practice, not a measure of health. It compares you with yourself, and with nothing else. Like the October tower, it's a game, not an approved training device: your instructor and your country's phraseology manual are the reference.

Demo

The video shows the consent screen, the calm minute, an exchange with the tower, the breathing guide and the timeline. The camera preview is blurred.

Code

dsiacci / readback

Readback

A radio practice partner for student and private pilots. A simulated tower talks to you, you read back out loud, and the camera follows your pulse and your breathing while you do, with the Presage SmartSpectra SDK. Before your readback, if your breathing has picked up while you listened, a short breathing guide offers itself: the tower can wait. After the circuit, a timeline shows which messages made your pulse climb, next to what the tower said and what you read back.

A mirror for practice, not a measure of health. Readback compares you only with yourself, with a calm minute taken at the start of each session. It makes no medical claim, shows no normal or abnormal value, and never says whether anyone is fit to fly. It is a practice game, not an approved training device: your flight instructor and your country's official phraseology manual are…

View on GitHub

Electron and plain JavaScript, under the Apache 2.0 licence. On a Mac with Apple Silicon: npm install, then npm run setup:tower once, your Presage key in ~/.config/readback/presage.key, and npm start. No camera at hand? The first screen offers simulated signals, labelled as such everywhere.

The tower is my October project, phraseology. Readback runs it unchanged, as a separate program on the same computer. Everything that reacts to the camera is new.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Readback asks the SDK for three signals, and nothing else:

Signal What the SDK gives What Readback does with it
Pulse rate an average over 12 seconds your reference, the live difference, and the climb after each message
Breathing rate an average over 30 seconds your reference during the calm minute
Chest movement the breathing waveform breaths counted while you listen, and the breathing guide

The wiring is the SDK's renderer entry point, with telemetry off:

const sdk = new SmartSpectraSDK({
  apiKey,  // read by the main process from a file in your home folder
  requestedMetrics: [MetricType.CHEST_BREATHING, MetricType.BREATHING_RATE, MetricType.PULSE_RATE],
  enableTelemetry: false,
});
sdk.on('metrics', (buf) => store.add(decodeMetrics(buf)));
sdk.on('validationStatus', (code) => showHint(code)); // "face the camera", "more light"…
await sdk.start(); // only after the consent screen

The most useful page was Presage's model card. It says the breathing rate doesn't hold while the person is talking. But a radio exchange is talking, a few seconds of listening, and talking again. There are never 30 quiet seconds.

So I used the chest movement instead, which the SDK streams next to the rate. Readback takes the moments when you are listening, removes the slow drift, and counts the breaths. The same count on the calm minute gives the reference. It's a rough count, but it's enough to notice that you breathe faster than at rest. Readback never shows a breathing number while you talk.

When that count is up by 4 breaths a minute or more, the breathing guide opens. You can change that threshold, or turn the guide off. It breathes four seconds in and six out, three times, and draws your own chest moving under the circle. The space bar skips it.

The timeline needed one correction. My first version ranked the messages by how high the pulse went above the calm minute. On the first test, with simulated signals, every message after a "negative" looked stressful, because the pulse was still up. Now a message's climb starts from the pulse at its first word. The level against the calm minute sits next to it.

Here is the timeline after my own circuit:

The clearance to land came first, with a climb of 14 beats per minute. The take-off clearance came third. Between them, the tower's request to read back the vacate instruction, which came right after landing, while my pulse was still up. Before both clearances, the breathing guide opened, and both times I skipped it to read back.

HRV and facial expressions are left out on purpose. HRV needs a full minute, longer than an exchange. And a label like "fear" on someone learning would be a judgement, with nothing true to add to the practice.

Prize Categories

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. Radio nerves are part of learning to fly, and the usual advice is "practise more", with nobody to practise with. Readback gives you a tower to practise with, and a mirror of what it does to you. The design follows from consent and from the SDK's limits: the camera opens only after you agree, the preview is blurred by default, the numbers are differences from your own calm minute, breathing is read only while you listen, and nothing is saved unless you ask.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The signal changes the conversation, not just a dashboard. When your breathing has picked up, the tower waits for you, and you watch your own chest move under the breathing circle. The tower's voice goes through a small radio filter with a squelch, and the screens use B612, the typeface designed for cockpit displays.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Consent first. The first screen says what is measured, what stays on the computer, what goes to Presage and how to stop. The camera opens only after "I agree, turn the camera on". The microphone is a separate choice; without it, you type your readbacks. Until you agree, the app refuses every camera and microphone request.
  • Visible and stoppable. "Camera on" and "Stop camera" stay at the top while the camera runs. Closing the window stops everything, and the camera turns off at the end of each circuit.
  • Images: never recorded, saved or sent by Readback.
  • Your voice: kept in memory while you hold the key, transcribed on the same computer by the tower, then dropped. Never written to disk.
  • Measurements: in memory during the session. Saved only if you press "Save on this computer", as a small file with your reference, the tower's messages, whether each readback was accepted, and the climbs. No image, no audio, no transcript. One button deletes every saved session.
  • What goes to Presage: the SDK computes pulse and breathing on the computer. It contacts Presage's service to check the API key and the plan. The SDK's usage telemetry is on by default; Readback turns it off.
  • No AI service. No language model writes anything about you. The tower's readback checks are plain rules.
  • Nothing else leaves the computer. The app's page can't reach the network. Setup downloads the packages and the speech models once; after that, the tower runs offline.

I built Readback to practise the long readbacks. My pulse cared about two short sentences.

Pilots: which radio call still gets you, years after the licence?

articles.title: I built a 3D open-world mythology game in the browser with just Three.js
articles.description: I'm a software developer, and for a while I'd been curious how far a browser could go with nothing...
articles.body_html:
I'm a software developer, and for a while I'd been curious how far a browser could go with nothing but Three.js and the Web Audio API. So I built a game to find out.

Devayan: The Ten Drops of Amrita is a free, open-source 3D action-exploration game inspired by Indian mythology. You free ten sacred sanctums on foot, awaken a flying Vimana (sky-chariot), and fly from the ground all the way to orbit to face an eclipse-lord.

🎮 Play it: GAME LINK
💻 Source (MIT): REPO LINK

The rules I set for myself

  • No game engine. Just Three.js.
  • No build step. Plain ES modules served as static files.
  • No external assets. Every model is built from geometry in code, and every sound is synthesized.

These limits kept the project small and made it deploy-anywhere. It's a handful of JS files and can be hosted on any static host.

Zero build tools

Browsers can load ES modules natively, and an import map lets import * as THREE from 'three' work without a bundler:

<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "three": "./libs/three.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module" src="./js/main.js"></script>

The one catch is that modules need HTTP, so python3 -m http.server is the whole dev setup.

Models without a modeling tool

Characters, temples, boats and the Vimana are all built from basic geometries combined in code. A low-poly, flat-shaded style hides the lack of detail and keeps a large world light enough for the browser. A big part of the charm comes from lighting and color choices, not mesh complexity.

Music without audio files

I wanted the world to feel Indian, which meant a tanpura drone and bansuri flute melodies, plus temple chimes and combat effects. Instead of shipping audio files, everything is generated in real time with the Web Audio API. That keeps the download tiny and lets the music be generated live. It was the most fun part of the project.

Flying from the ground into space

I didn't want a loading screen between the world and orbit. The sky blends from day into space as you climb, using a blend factor based on altitude:

const spaceBlend = THREE.MathUtils.clamp(
  (vehicle.position.y - 28) / (spaceAltitude - 28), 0, 1
);

That one value drives the sky color, fog and the switch into the orbital combat arena, so the transition feels continuous.

Game design wrapped around a story

The ten sanctums, three unlockable "astras" and the orbital boss all come from one simple legend: ten drops of divine nectar, an eclipse-demon who wants them, and you in between. Having a story gave me an answer every time I wasn't sure what to build next. Progress is saved in localStorage, with an atlas for fast travel between freed sanctums.

What I'd do next

There's plenty to improve, and I'd love your thoughts:

  • Bridges or clearer paths early on, since water can block new players
  • A more convincing space environment when you reach orbit
  • A second phase for the boss fight
  • Performance testing across low-end laptops and phones

Try it and tell me what you think

The game is free, ad-free and open source. If you play it, I'd really like to hear about performance on your device and how the controls feel. And if you want to read the code, everything is in the repo.

Three JS post

Thanks for reading! 🙏

articles.title: I built a CLI that turns any place on Earth into a pixel-art diorama
articles.description: Type a place, get an isometric pixel-art poster, video or GIF built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps data.
articles.body_html:
I wanted a picture of the street I grew up on, drawn like an old isometric game. I couldn't find a tool that did it from real map data, so I wrote one.

npx dioramap "Eiffel Tower, Paris" -t night

About ten seconds later there's a poster in the current folder. A place name, a street address or a pair of coordinates all work.

Where the data comes from

  • Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's geocoder, finds the place.
  • Roads, water, parks and land use come from OpenFreeMap vector tiles.
  • Buildings come from Overture Maps, which merges OpenStreetMap with Microsoft and Google footprints. Towns that are thin on OpenStreetMap still get their buildings this way.

The buildings are read straight out of Overture's PMTiles file and the rest from static vector tiles. There's no server of mine in the middle, so there's no API key and no rate limit.

Heights and roofs

Buildings keep their mapped parts, heights and roof shapes. That's how the Eiffel Tower gets its tapering legs and St Peter's gets its dome. When nobody mapped a height, I guess one from the footprint and how built-up the area around it is.

Making it look like pixel art

three.js renders the scene into a render target at a third of the final size, using the 2:1 camera angle pixel artists use. On top of that go outlines, sun shadows, lit windows, trees and cars. Then the image is scaled up with nearest-neighbour filtering, so every edge stays hard.

There's no AI model anywhere in the pipeline. That's why it never comes out blurry.

Video and GIF

--video makes an MP4 where the flat street map rises into the city building by building, then night falls and the lights come on. The headless browser encodes the H.264 frames with WebCodecs and I write the MP4 container myself, so you don't need ffmpeg.

npx dioramap "Dubai Marina" -t night --video
npx dioramap "Rialto Bridge, Venice" --gif

What it can't do

How good it looks depends on the map data. Big cities come out great. A village nobody has mapped in detail looks sparse, and dioramap won't invent buildings to fill it in.

Try it

You need Node 20 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium installed.

npx dioramap "your street, your city"

The code is MIT licensed: https://github.com/omlahore/dioramap

If you render your hometown, I'd like to see it.

articles.title: Systole - your heartbeat is the drum machine
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge What I Built Systole is a musical...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
What I Built
Systole is a musical instrument that knows exactly one thing about you: what your body is doing right now.

You sit in front of a webcam, press Start, and it plays. Your heartbeat is the drummer - every systolic upstroke SmartSpectra finds in the arterial pressure waveform fires a kick drum and a ring of light, and the interval between your actual beats is the tempo of the piece. Your breathing opens the orchestra: as your chest rises a low-pass filter opens and the pad swells, and as you exhale it closes again. HRV picks the mode - open major pentatonic when you're calmer than your own session baseline, minor pentatonic when you're more charged. Pulse rate picks the key, and a smile adds a bell.

No wearable. No controller. No microphone. No "tap here to play". The interface is your autonomic nervous system.

The Systole instrument running: a glowing orb pulsing with the beat, a tempo readout of 73 bpm captioned "the kit is on your pulse", live pulse and breathing readouts, and the arterial pressure waveform along the bottom

That shot comes from a headless CI run on a machine with no camera, so the app badges
it SIMULATED - the demo video above is the real thing, with a real pulse in front of a
real lens.

The moment I was aiming for: you sit still, slightly bored, and then the kick lands on your own heartbeat. Not near it, not at a tempo somebody typed in - on the beat the SDK just heard in your face. People stop talking when that happens. Then they laugh, their pulse moves, and the music moves with it.

A single unbroken take, with the camera preview, the live pulse number and the music all on screen at once, so you can hear the tempo tracking the reading. Two moments worth watching for:

0:20-0:45 - the kick locks onto the detected beats. The caption under the big tempo readout switches from "tempo from pulse rate while the waveform settles" to "N beats heard in the pressure wave - the kit is on your pulse". That's the waveform driving it, not a reported average.
1:10 - I cover the lens for three seconds. Signal quality collapses, the pad closes down and the bells stop, because the app refuses to keep playing to a body it can no longer see. Uncovering brings it back.
There's also a landing page at SITE_URL describing the app, the signal mapping and the privacy design. Systole needs Electron and the native SmartSpectra runtime, so the page describes the instrument rather than running it - clone the repo to play.

Code
github.com/SarthakPatil18/Systole - MIT licensed, public, with setup instructions in the README.

Bash

git clone https://github.com/SarthakPatil18/Systole.git systole
cd systole
npm install
npm start # paste your Presage API key into the consent sheet
npm test # 18 logic tests + a headless run of the real renderer
Stack: Electron plus the renderer-side @smartspectra/node-sdk binding, esbuild for the renderer bundle, and hand-written Web Audio and Canvas 2D - no audio library, no charting library, no UI framework.

Three layers of tests, all runnable without a camera:

npm test - 18 logic tests (musical mapping, breath normalisation, beat detection including the dicrotic-notch regression below) plus a headless run that fakes the DOM, canvas and Web Audio and executes the actual bundled renderer.
npm run check:sdk - loads the real SDK native runtime, proves the metric list is accepted, and drives start() to the authentication boundary.
SYSTOLE_SCREENSHOT / SYSTOLE_SMOKE_JS - scriptable headless UI runs on a virtual display. Every screenshot in this post came out of one of those.
How It Responds to Human Signals
Systole requests [...breathingMetrics, ...cardioMetrics, MetricType.EXPRESSIONS] and uses four of the SDK's signals in genuinely different ways:

Signal What it does in the instrument
Arterial pressure trace Beat detection -> kick drum + light ring. Beat-to-beat interval is the tempo.
Chest + abdomen traces Normalised into a breath phase -> pad filter cutoff and gain. You hear yourself breathe.
HRV (Baevsky index) Compared to a slow baseline of your own session -> chooses the pentatonic mode.
Pulse rate Sets the root of the piece and covers the tempo while the waveform is still settling.
Expressions A smile raises the probability of a bell ornament. Optional - the app rebuilds without it if your plan doesn't include face metrics.
Validation status + confidence Fades the pad, suppresses new notes, shows the SDK's hint in plain language.
The integration is deliberately the boring, recommended one for Electron:

main.js
calls bindSmartSpectraIpc(win) and points webPreferences.preload at @smartspectra/node-sdk/preload. One SDK instance per window, torn down on close.
The renderer constructs SmartSpectraSDK from @smartspectra/node-sdk/renderer, so the SDK owns capture and hands back a MediaStream via streamAvailable for the preview. The microphone is never requested.
Metrics arrive as protobuf on the metrics event and are decoded with the SDK's own decodeMetrics from @smartspectra/node-sdk/messages.
If the plan rejects expression metrics (kConfigurationFailed / kMetricNotAuthorized), the app rebuilds without them and says so instead of dying.
Then the interesting part.

  1. Beats, not averages. The SDK gives a waveform, not beat events, so
    signal-engine.js
    finds the systolic upstroke itself: a sample has to clear the recent mean plus 35% of the swing and 72% of the recent peak-to-peak range, then fall back near the mean before it can re-arm. That amplitude gate is what stops the dicrotic notch counting as a second heartbeat - the bug that doubles your tempo. There's a regression test pinning it. The resulting intervals go through a 7-sample median, so one bad frame can't rewrite the groove, and the median interval is the tempo.

  2. Breath as a continuous control. Chest and abdomen traces are normalised against an 8-second rolling min/max into a breathPhase (0 = exhaled, 1 = inhaled), smoothed, and mapped to filter cutoff and pad gain. You can hear yourself breathe within two seconds, long before the 30-second breathing-rate window completes.

  3. HRV relative to you. Baevsky's stress index only means something against a personal baseline, so the app builds one from your own session (a slow 2% EMA) and compares against it. Crossing +25% of baseline shifts the mode darker; sitting 15% under it opens the bright one. Nobody's absolute number decides anything.

  4. Quality is audible. A quality value from the SDK's confidence scores and validationStatus control pad brightness and volume and suppress new notes. Bad light, motion, or no face means a thinner, quieter piece, with the SDK's validation hint shown as plain language ("Too dark - face a window or a lamp"). The instrument degrades honestly instead of inventing a reading.

Everything is scheduled with Web Audio lookahead (25 ms tick, 120 ms ahead) so the music never stutters when a frame is slow, and the audio graph is built once and retuned rather than reallocated on chord changes.

Prize Categories
Entering both - the honest fit is somewhere in between.

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The thing that made me build it: a pulse is something you cannot perceive without a device touching you, and music is the one medium where "here is what your body is doing" needs no explanation. Your heart becomes a drummer - not a visualisation of a drummer, an actual one, playing in time with you. The delight is realising the room is being kept in time by your own body, and the fact that the same ninety seconds makes people lean in, go quiet, then start tapping.

Best Thoughtful Real-World Use. What I removed on purpose points at who this is for. There is no wearable and no hands - nothing to strap on, hold, tap or charge - so the instrument is playable by people who can't grip a controller, who can't wear something on their wrist, or find both sensory-hostile, and by anyone who simply won't wear a heart-rate sensor. It also shows the signal without interpreting it: no scores, no stress level, no "you seem anxious", no diagnosis. For someone prone to over-monitoring their own body, "listen to this and breathe" is a kinder interface than a number that judges them. And because the mapping only ever nudges between gentle pentatonic modes, nothing the app detects can produce an alarming sound - the worst case of a wild reading is slightly odd music, which is the right failure mode for a wellness toy.

Consent and Data Handling
Full detail in PRIVACY.md; the summary:

Consent gate. Nothing touches the camera until the person has read a plain-language sheet, ticked an explicit consent checkbox ("my camera will be used to measure my pulse and breathing while Systole is running") and pressed Begin. The tick is per-session and is not stored - the next launch asks again.

The consent sheet: what the camera is used for, that nothing is recorded, the API key field, an opt-in diagnostics checkbox and the required consent checkbox

In
main.js
the camera is granted only for a video-only permission request, only from the app's own bundled file:// page; audio requests and any non-local origin are denied. Navigation and popups are blocked so the window can't be steered somewhere else. macOS's own prompt and camera indicator stay in force, and Stop releases the camera immediately.

Processing. Frames go from the renderer to the SmartSpectra SDK in the app's main process; measurement is on-device. Systole itself records nothing: no video, no audio, no vitals history, no session log, no analytics, no account, no identifiers. The API key is held in memory for the session and never written to disk; it is sent only to Presage's authenticated API.

Network. The only traffic Systole causes is the SDK's API-key authentication and subscription check - no video and no measured values in that request. There is no cloud service, no LLM call, and no optional AI feature in this app.

SDK telemetry - reversed default, disclosed. Presage's SDK telemetry is on by default; Systole sets enableTelemetry from an unchecked box on the consent sheet, so it is off unless the person opts in. If enabled, the SDK sends aggregate measurement-session summaries (SDK build, platform/device/arch, session shape, throughput and startup timings, counts of quality warnings, coarse error codes, a timestamp) and full device-readiness diagnostic reports - no raw frames and no measured physiological values. Those requests are authenticated, so they can be correlated with an account and shouldn't be called anonymous. Readiness reports live in Presage's private diagnostic storage with no automatic expiry; deletion follows Presage's policies. Turning it off means the SDK starts no telemetry session at all.

Retention and deletion. There is nothing to retain: quit the app and the session is gone, no server-side copy of measurements exists, and no files are written. For Presage-side diagnostic records, contact support@presagetech.com.

Not a medical device. Pulse, breathing, HRV and expression signals are used here for wellness and entertainment. Systole makes no diagnosis or treatment claims, takes no medical decisions, has no alerting or emergency behaviour, and is not for covert or non-consensual monitoring - it measures only the person who consented, in front of their own camera, with a visible indicator, and it never runs hidden or in the background. The consent sheet and the side rail both say so, inside the app, not just here.

articles.title: For 61 Years, Kodak Ran on a 13-Month Calendar — So I Rebuilt It for 2027 in Vanilla JS
articles.description: Between 1928 and 1989, one of the largest industrial companies on Earth ran its internal payroll,...
articles.body_html:
Between 1928 and 1989, one of the largest industrial companies on Earth ran its internal payroll, manufacturing schedules, and financial reporting on a 13-month × 28-day calendar.

Eastman Kodak adopted Moses Cotsworth’s International Fixed Calendar (IFC) so every accounting period would have the exact same number of days (28), four complete weeks, and identical weekday-to-date mapping year after year. Every month started on the exact same weekday, every weekend hit the exact same columns, and monthly reporting never suffered from 28-vs-31-day Gregorian distortion.

To make space for the 13th month, Month 07: SOL sits right between June and July (June 18 – July 15), centered around the June Solstice. The 365th day (December 31) becomes Year Day, standing outside the seven-day week so the whole calendar stays symmetrical.

Ahead of 2027, I rebuilt this entire system as a zero-dependency web explorer, live birthday converter, and print-ready wall archive: SOL-2027 Explorer.

Why Vanilla JS + Zero Build Step Won Here

Calendar tools fail when they feel sluggish or require signup walls. The core math fits inside a single isomorphic zero-dependency script, so every interaction — birthday lookup, 365-day diagonal inspection, and instant 1080×1920 story-card export — runs locally in microseconds.

Mapping any 2027 Gregorian (month, day) onto the 13-month grid uses precomputed cumulative month lengths (CUMULATIVE_DAYS):

  1. Compute 1-based day-of-year doy in [1..365] (2027 is a common year starting Friday, Jan 1).
  2. Handle doy === 365 explicitly as Year Day (December 31, intercalary holiday).
  3. For 1 <= doy <= 364:
    • ifcMonthIndex = Math.floor((doy - 1) / 28) (0 = Jan … 6 = SOL … 12 = Dec)
    • ifcDay = ((doy - 1) % 28) + 1

Look at what happens visually when you plot all 365 days in a 13×28 matrix: the Gregorian 1st of every month marches cleanly down the matrix like a diagonal staircase, because every Gregorian 30- or 31-day month overflows the clean 28-day boundary by 2 or 3 cells:

  • July 1 actually becomes SOL 14
  • October 31 becomes OCT 24
  • December 25 becomes DEC 23

Even February 29 leaplings have a historical Cotsworth–Eastman rule supported directly in the converter: in leap years like 2028, Gregorian Feb 29 becomes Day 60 of 366 — fixed forever on IFC MARCH 4 (Wednesday) — while the IFC inserts its own intercalary Leap Day at JUNE 29, sitting outside the seven-day week right before SOL 1.

An Unexpected 2027 Astronomy Coincidence: Literally 13 New Moons

While computing UTC lunar phases and solar solstices/equinoxes for 2027 using Jean Meeus astronomical algorithms (cross-checked with PyEphem), I noticed a rare gift for 2027 calendar nerds:

2027 has exactly 13 astronomical New Moons (Jan 7 20:25 UTC through Dec 27 20:13 UTC) — meaning one New Moon lands inside every single one of the 13 IFC months.

  • 01 · January (Jan 1 – Jan 28): Jan 7 · 20:25 UTC
  • 02 · February (Jan 29 – Feb 25): Feb 6 · 15:57 UTC
  • 03 · March (Feb 26 – Mar 25): Mar 8 · 09:30 UTC
  • 04 · April (Mar 26 – Apr 22): Apr 6 · 23:52 UTC
  • 05 · May (Apr 23 – May 20): May 6 · 10:59 UTC
  • 06 · June (May 21 – Jun 17): Jun 4 · 19:41 UTC
  • 07 · SOL (Jun 18 – Jul 15): Jul 4 · 03:03 UTC (+ June Solstice on SOL 4)
  • 08 · July (Jul 16 – Aug 12): Aug 2 · 10:06 UTC
  • 09 · August (Aug 13 – Sep 9): Aug 31 · 17:42 UTC
  • 10 · September (Sep 10 – Oct 7): Sep 30 · 02:37 UTC
  • 11 · October (Oct 8 – Nov 4): Oct 29 · 13:37 UTC
  • 12 · November (Nov 5 – Dec 2): Nov 28 · 03:25 UTC
  • 13 · December (Dec 3 – Dec 30): Dec 27 · 20:13 UTC

Client-Side Swiss Typography & 1080×1920 Story Cards

Because the converter itself is the viral hook ("Wait, I was born on SOL 14?!"), I built a client-side HTML5 <canvas> exporter inside the web app. Click Download 1080×1920 Story Card after converting your birthday, and it renders a high-contrast Swiss Editorial or Midnight Celestial card straight to PNG on-device — zero server rendering, zero upload latency, zero watermarks.

And for people who want the system off-screen (especially ADHD visual planners, cycle-syncing trackers, and studio desks), every date cell pairs its large IFC numeral with its exact real-world Gregorian cross-date in the corner — available both as a $0+ Letter/A4 Starter PDF and printed physical editions via SOL-2027 Guides & Editions.

Try Your Date

  • Interactive Birthday Converter & Full 13×28 Matrix: https://sol-2027.vercel.app
  • Visual Field Guides & Print Editions: https://sol-2027.vercel.app/2027

articles.title: Why NFD normalization quietly breaks Icelandic search
articles.description: If you have ever built search for a language with diacritics, you have probably reached for...
articles.body_html:
If you have ever built search for a language with diacritics, you have probably reached for this:

const fold = s => s.normalize('NFD').replace(/\p{M}/gu, '').toLowerCase();

Decompose, strip the combining marks, lowercase. It is the standard trick and it works beautifully for French, Spanish, Portuguese.

For Icelandic it silently does half the job, and the half it misses is the half that matters.

What NFD actually does

NFD decomposes precomposed characters into a base letter plus combining marks. á becomes a + U+0301, and stripping the mark leaves a. Same for é í ó ú ý ö.

Now try it on these:

fold('þjónusta')  // 'þjonusta'  — þ survived
fold('góður')     // 'goður'     — ð survived
fold('æfing')     // 'æfing'     — æ survived

þ (thorn), ð (eth) and æ (ash) are not precomposed characters. They are distinct letters with no decomposition mapping. NFD leaves them exactly where they were, and your "normalized" index still contains characters that no one is going to type on a US keyboard.

Why that is a real problem and not a cosmetic one

Icelanders on foreign keyboard layouts substitute. þ becomes th. ð becomes d. æ becomes ae. This is not a rare edge case — it is what the query log looks like.

So a user searching thjonusta finds nothing, while your index sits there holding þjonusta, which is neither the original nor what anyone typed.

In a large language you get rescued by the search engine's own fuzzy matching and a mountain of query data. In a language with a few hundred thousand speakers there is no such safety net. Nobody has trained a "did you mean" model on your queries. If your matching layer does not handle it, it does not get handled.

The fix

An explicit map, applied to both sides:

const FOLD = {
  'á':'a', 'é':'e', 'í':'i', 'ó':'o', 'ú':'u', 'ý':'y',
  'ð':'d', 'þ':'th', 'æ':'ae', 'ö':'o'
};

const fold = s =>
  s.toLowerCase().replace(/[áéíóúýðþæö]/g, c => FOLD[c]);

Lowercase first so uppercase forms are covered by the same map.

Three things worth knowing before you ship this.

þ → th changes the string length.** One character becomes two. If you are highlighting matches by index into the original string, your offsets are now wrong. Either fold a copy and keep a position map, or highlight on the unfolded text with a separate pass.

Fold the query the same way, at the same time.** The invariant is that both sides pass through identical code. The moment the index is folded at build time and the query is folded by a slightly different function at request time, you get failures that are miserable to reproduce.

Do not fold what you display. This belongs in the matching layer only. Nothing the reader sees should lose its diacritics — góður and goður are not the same word, and showing the second one looks broken to a native speaker.

Sorting is a separate problem

While you are here: Icelandic alphabetical order puts þ, æ and ö at the end, after z. A naive .sort() on code points gets this wrong, and so does folding, since folding has already thrown the information away.

list.sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b, 'is'));

Use the locale-aware comparison on the original strings. Fold for matching, compare for ordering, and keep the two apart.

Where this came from

I wrote this for a retrieval index on an Icelandic site I run, where the whole search layer is one plain-text file and a Cloudflare Worker — no embeddings, no vector database. The diacritic folding took more iterations than any other part of it, which is why it seemed worth writing down.

If you work in a language with letters outside the Latin-1 comfort zone, the general lesson is probably the same: check what your normalization actually does to your alphabet before trusting it. The standard recipe was written for a different set of letters.
